title: From Tokyo to Herat
desc:
Japanese Near East Dispatch Force, Herat, September 18, 1979
________________________________________
At dawn, the blood-colored dawn
Fujita stood at the edge of the camp, staring at the dusky desert in the distance. The morning air was still heavy, with a strong smell of sand and dust, and he habitually
raised his hand to cover the sun in front of him. The sky of Herat is vast, but the vast desert is always suffocating. He put down the telescope in his hand, and the
corners of his mouth curled slightly: "Maybe, this is my fate." ”
Since the order was issued by Tokyo, Japan's Near East Dispatch Army has appeared like a ghost in this "imperial graveyard". Fujita does not deny that he did not come here
for the sake of "freedom" or "justice" – he was here to defend the interests of the empire, to hold the boundaries of power that had been eroded by Japan on a global
scale. War, for Fujita, has long ceased to be a pan-Asianist romance, but a mechanized chess game.
________________________________________
At 9:30 a.m., the tide of battle remained unshaken
"Your task is to provide them with assistance and support their combat effectiveness." Fujita did not have a trace of expression on his face when he conveyed the
instructions of his superiors to his subordinates. The Japanese military's position is clear – to support pro-Japanese forces in Afghanistan and to ensure that the
situation here is not biased in favor of Russia or Western countries. However, the reality is more complex than any strategy.
Every time he interacts with the Afghan armed forces, Fujita feels an inexplicable sense of oppression. The eyes of the soldiers armed in these places were full of
confusion and anger. The land of Afghanistan will not easily accept foreign invaders, regardless of their appearance. In his interactions with these locals, Fujita sensed
their fears and their dislike for Japan's history, the empire that invaded China and Southeast Asia.
Still, he firmly believes, "This place has to be controlled by us." It was for the sake of the "greater future", for the sake of the Japanese Empire to which he was loyal.
________________________________________
At 2:00 p.m., the atmosphere was heavy
Soon after, Fujita received orders to lead his troops to a village south of Herat to provide support. Through intelligence, they learned that pro-Soviet forces in the
region were active and that tough measures had to be taken. However, this is not a simple battle.
There was a suffocating atmosphere in the village. Fujita and his men made their way through the crowd and into a humble dwelling. Inside, several ragged villagers bowed
their heads and remained silent, their eyes uneasy. Fujita couldn't help but realize that the eyes of these villagers were full of fear of war, but more often than not, a
deep rejection of outside forces.
"Our mission is not for the people here." Fujita whispered to the lieutenant accompanying him, "This is just so that Japan's influence will not be weakened." ”
What he didn't say was: "After all, we are just pawns of the empire." ”
________________________________________
6:15 p.m., silence in the cold wind
Back at camp, Fujita stood outside the tent and felt the cold wind from Herat blowing in the desert. This is a picture that has been repeated every day since he arrived in
Afghanistan. Anxiety and tension during the day are accompanied by deep loneliness at night. Despite the hundreds of troops and colleagues around him, Fujita knew that
they all had the same sense of depression in their hearts - this was a war with no winners, and they were nothing more than a group of unchosen warriors trapped in this
desert.
He recalls his time in Tokyo, the glory and dreams of the past, the high spirits of the former Japanese Empire, and everything seems so hopeful. But now, he faces a land
of death and despair, and every inch of Afghanistan is making him lose himself.
Fujita stood for a moment, then jerked around and walked into the depths of the camp.
He clearly knew that he, like all the soldiers on this battlefield, had long since left the so-called "glory" and entered a reality full of mud and blood. And all this,
perhaps, can never be clearly explained, and it is impossible to really stop.
________________________________________
12:00 p.m., the struggle in my heart
As the night wore on, the lights in the camp were gradually extinguished. Fujita lay on a simple bed, his eyes fixed on the roof of the tent. Through the faint light, he
could see the crooked shadows—he knew there was no way back. It was not just for the sake of winning or losing the war, but also for the future of the Japanese Empire, or,
for the fate that he now had to face.
"What is the point of my coming here?" Fujita asked silently in his heart.
No one answered him, and his heart slowly grew cold. Perhaps, this is the truth of war-"

title: Like a ghost
desc:
Co-Prosperity Sphere Observer Group in Afghanistan, Secret Service Unofficial Contact, Herat, 8 May 1980
________________________________________
8:10 a.m
He walked through the dust and sand of the streets and the orange morning light, not fast or slow. Beneath you is the scene of an explosion that was dealt with just
yesterday. The secret service left no traces, only the conclusion: "Non-Chinese assets accidentally touched the misleading materials laid by the United States." ”
He wore a round hat and gray civilian clothes, and hid among merchants, clergy, and advisors. No one knows his name, only one code name: Hiyama No. 2. This is the name of
Tokyo, not Herat.
He walked into a teahouse. The landlord had already left a letter under the counter, the letter was written in Turkish, but the paper was the "silkworm white type"
characteristic of East Asian paper mills. He didn't open the letter, just ordered a cup of black tea, drank it, and left.
________________________________________
11:47 a.m
He met with the nephew of a local pro-Japanese warlord at an abandoned French-style church on the outskirts of Herat.
"We need your people to control that drain." Hiyama whispered, "It's not for irrigation, it's for the three villages on the map." ”
"The Germans are also bidding." The nephew reminded him.

title: Thirteenth signature
desc:
Advisory Mission of the Russian Federation in Afghanistan, Diary of Operations R-7 in the Theater of Operations, April 1, 1981
Location: Nangarhar Province, on the periphery of the buffer zone in southern Ghazni
________________________________________
2:06 a.m
When he opened his eyes, he was still sitting at the aluminium war table, mud on his boots, dirt on his trouser legs, and his fingers still clutching the bitten pen.
The folder was spread out, and the red cover was printed with nine black letters: "Letter of Authorization for Chemical Cleanup Operations".
He had already signed a similar order twelve times.
Today is the thirteenth time.
But he didn't put pen to paper for a long time.
The radio in the corner of the table was also broadcasting a headquarters briefing: "We must quickly weaken the armed will of the south and cut off its logistical contacts
with the German side." The tone was as smooth as the weather forecast.
He closed his eyes and saw only the video sent yesterday - the crowd at the entrance of the village, the guerrillas mixed with the refugees, the children lining up with
empty pots to get water, and a woman holding the child screaming at the camera.
She speaks Pashto. But he understood.
She was scolding them, "Where is your God? ”
________________________________________
9:40 a.m
The airdrop is complete. The flight unit, codenamed "Igor", dropped four tanks of improved CL-34 gas. According to intelligence, more than 60 unarmed civilians were in the
targeted area with suspected guerrillas.
"It's not very likely." The deputy consultant wrote in the report.
"A necessary price." The chief of staff said from the side.
He stood in front of the remote monitoring platform, staring at the white mist wafting out, his palm pressed against the cold glass surface. The drone's picture begins to
blur, with noise, flickering, and finally black and white.
He knew that there was no longer a sound of breathing.
________________________________________
1:22 p.m
Lunch was canned, dry cakes, and sugar water.
He didn't move.
"Do you know what the U.S. military did in Kandahar?" One young consultant said, "We don't even do a hundredth of what they do." ”
He did not respond. Just put his hand in the pocket of his military coat and pinched the carbon paper—it had his signature on it, thirteenth.
The handwriting is more stable than the previous twelve.
That's what makes him sick the most.
________________________________________
6:04 p.m
HQ issued a commendation: "The R-7 acted quickly and decisively, effectively deterring the local armed activity. It is recommended that the authority for asymmetric
operations be continuously expanded. ”
He sat on the slope at the back of the camp, looking out at the valley in the distance, which had been labeled "neutral" by military intelligence. The wind blew from the
mountain pass, with a faint sour smell. He didn't know if it was a real gas residue or a hallucination in his own nasal cavity.
"You didn't do anything wrong." The adjutant said, "It was HQ who asked us to do this." ”
He suddenly asked, "Who is HQ?" ”
The adjutant was stunned.
"Have you ever seen HQ's face? Do you know if HQ has a wife? Do they also dream of those charred bodies in the middle of the night? ”
He paused, and his voice was extremely soft:
"I don't want to dream of that well anymore."
________________________________________
11:59 a.m
He finally returned to the tent and took out the carbon paper one by one, a copy of each order. Twelve are complete, and the thirteenth still bears fingerprints.
He began to burn them one by one.
The light of the fire reflected the tent like a tomb. He knelt on the sand, the last one unburned—"...... Authorized to immediately carry out the clean-up ......" The line
struggled in the fire, as if begging for mercy.
He finally cried.
Not because of remorse.
Because he knew he would sign the fourteenth.

title: German Air Force Volunteer Corps · Afghanistan Theater · Tactical Pilot Action Log
desc:
June 1, 1982 · Badakhshan region, area of REGEN-E operation
________________________________________
06:04
When he opened his eyes, there was blood outside the window.
No, it's the rising sun. But his first reaction was the orange color after the alarm light flashed. He couldn't figure it out anymore.
On the sheets were salt stains from the sweat he had done last night. In the dream, there was a house that was on fire, and a figure fell from the roof, holding a baby in
his hand. He woke up with his hands clenched, as if he was still trying to hold on to something.
He sat up, his throat tight.
The captain told him that today's mission was just a "regular sweep". Clearing of guerrilla transit points in a certain mountainous area.
"There are no civilians," said the captain, "where are the civilians?" Did you see those radio navigators? It's just a bunch of cowsheds. ”
________________________________________
08:12
Launch. He turned on the HUD, and the system calmly listed the coordinates of the target, the state of the weapon, the wind speed.
He began to pray that something was wrong. At least then he can fly off. Unfortunately, everything works fine.
"In the REGEN-E area, the enemy is expected to be transferred at the western entrance of the K valley and destroy all structures."
He saw the crowd as he swooped.
Not soldiers. Not partisans.
It's a group of people. An old man, a child, a woman was washing clothes by the river, and a child was standing on a stone and waving at him.
He froze. Hand over the release key. The brain stops working.
A reprimand came from the communication channel:
"What are you waiting for? We don't want to take back the baby Madonna, the pilot, to carry out your orders. ”
He pressed it.
He pressed.
________________________________________
08:16
In the dust from the explosion, he saw the child's hand—and in that moment, he did.
But when I looked again, the child was gone. There was just a pile of charred and blackened coals.
He suddenly wondered if he had misremembered.
"Perhaps...... The kid was somewhere else. ”
But a voice echoed coldly in his head: You killed him with your own hands.
________________________________________
13:00
Afternoon. He returned to the base. The officer came over and patted him: "The task was done neatly, cleanly, precisely. ”
The corners of his mouth twitched, and he nodded.
No one mentioned the child. No one mentioned the woman.
Their names, he never known.
________________________________________
15:25
He sat outside the barracks, the sun falling on his knees. He suddenly remembered that his mother was a washerwoman when she was young, and that she knelt by the river to
rub her clothes exactly like the woman this morning.
He covered his face with his palm. That's not self-blame. It was some kind of deeper fear.
- What if he killed his own mother? Own children? Your own neighbors?
But he immediately retorted to himself: "But they are not." They are supporters behind enemy lines, potential threats, saboteurs of imperial security. ”
He took a deep breath.
Then he saw a figure approaching, a girl in a red dress, with dark skin and no shoes on her feet. She walked slowly, step by step.
He slammed to his feet—nothing. The camp was empty.
His back was soaked with sweat.
________________________________________
18:46
He lay in bed, unable to sleep. Fingers grasp the fabric little by little on the side of the pillow.
There was a knock on the door. He got up and opened it, and there was no one outside the door.
He turned around, and there was a child sitting on the bed. Black hair, big eyes, gray all over, holding a broken ball in his hand.
He glared at the child. The kid stared at him too.
Time stood still for a full twenty seconds.
He slammed the light on.
Nothing.
Nothing.
________________________________________
21:10
He wrote his last words in his diary:
"We thought we were dropping bombs, but in fact we were bones."
He put down his pen and looked out the window at the starry sky.
A meteor streaked by.
He instinctively prayed, "If there are gods, let me never see them again in my dreams." ”
But he knew that the god might have died in that village.
Or maybe just lie on the edge of the blown up well, with your eyes still open, looking at him...

title: Under the sand, the rose has not bloomed
desc:
October 10, 1983 · Northern Valley of Badakhshan · The 7th guerrilla stronghold of the Afghan National Liberation Front
________________________________________
04:26
When he woke up, the sky was still dark. The ground was as cold as stone. He pulled his hand from under the blanket, his fingers frozen stiff. The gun rested beside him,
and he subconsciously shook it - the metal was as cold as a knife. He didn't move, and after holding it for a while, it seemed that he could still feel some blood flowing.
Not far away was Hamid, curled up in a broken carpet and coughing. They lost a supply point last night, and only four escaped. The other ten were either dead or didn't
know where they had gone.
Someone called his mother's name in a dream and whimpered in a low voice. When he thought of his mother, he noticed that his face was wet.
But not because of crying, but because there is blood in the dream and a baby crying. He knelt in the rubble, his hands covered with broken bones. He couldn't save the
child.
________________________________________
06:02
They planted explosives in the mountain passes and prepared to ambush a Russian supply convoy.
He deftly tied the lead with his fingers and bit the stem of hay in his mouth. He suddenly laughed.
Hamid asked, "How?" ”
"I also played with these lines when I was a kid...... At that time, I was making kites at home. Now, I'm still making kites. ”
Hamid didn't laugh, just looked at him: "You're crazy. ”
He nodded, "Maybe." ”
________________________________________
10:18
The mine exploded.
Their ambush was successful, but at an extremely high cost. At the moment of the explosion, he stood too close and was stunned. When I woke up, there was scorched earth
all around. The three team members lay down, not moving. One of his heads was broken, and his eyes were still looking at him. It was Rashid, who was only eighteen years
old.
He looked up, and there was a living one in the distance, leaning against the stone and gasping. He rushed over, only to find that it was a Russian soldier, with blood all
over his face, half of his teeth missing, and a song in his mouth.
He raised his gun and aimed it at him.
The man looked up, the corners of his mouth twitching, and he seemed to say, "Mom." ”
He froze.
He fired.
He killed a man who sang and said "Mommy".
________________________________________
14:30
They returned to their hiding place, and it began to snow.
He sat by the fire, roasting his frozen hands.
The firelight flickered. He saw the Russian soldier sitting across from him.
He raised his gun again, only to find that the muzzle of the gun was rusty. There was blood sticking to the trigger, whether it was his own or someone else's, he couldn't
tell the difference.
The soldier spoke, and it was still the same sentence: "Mom." ”
He closed his eyes, and when he opened them again, there was only a pile of empty ammunition boxes across the fire.
________________________________________
16:55
They heard on the radio that a Pamir village in the east had been bombed yesterday. More than a dozen people died, and many children were not found.
Someone scolded: "Bastard German." ”
He didn't speak. He suddenly wanted to ask: "Are you scolding Germans, or Russians, Americans, or Japanese?" ”
– or, are we ourselves?
Because they buried the explosives in advance, they hid the barracks, and they robbed the supplies. Before the village was flattened, was it because they had been hiding
there for the night?
He slammed into his feet and rushed out of the hole, trying to throw up. But I can't spit it out.
The stomach is empty, and so is the heart.
________________________________________
19:20
During the night, he had a dream.
In the dream, he went back to his childhood. My father washed clothes by the river, and my mother made bread in the house. He ran like a child, chasing a kite over stones,
grass and hillsides.
Suddenly, there was a loud bang, and he fell.
It's not him, it's the kite that broke the string and fell into the fire.
The kite is free.
He opened his eyes, and there was silence all around. He thought he was dead.
But he's still alive.
He sat up slowly, and there was only one sentence left in his head:
"What we have watered with blood is not freedom, but a deeper hell. May Allah have mercy on us. ”
________________________________________
21:10
The night was eerily quiet. He held the gun in his hand, and the barrel still had the body temperature of the Russian soldier - not the real temperature, the temperature
he imagined.
He fired a shot at the wall. Bullet casings hit the ground.
"Boom."
Hamid was startled and rushed over and asked, "What are you doing?" ”
He turned around and smiled on the verge of collapse:
"I just want to be sure...... We're not in Serrer..."

During the night, he had a dream.
In the dream, he went back to his childhood. My father washed clothes by the river, and my mother made bread in the house. He ran like a child, chasing a kite over stones,
grass and hillsides.
Suddenly, there was a loud bang, and he fell.
It's not him, it's the kite that broke the string and fell into the fire.
The kite is free.
He opened his eyes, and there was silence all around. He thought he was dead.
But he's still alive.
He sat up slowly, and there was only one sentence left in his head:
"What we have watered with blood is not freedom, but a deeper hell. May Allah have mercy on us. ”

title: Meat grinder
desc:
The rubber edges of the gas mask pressed against Ivan Ivanovich Ivanov's cheek, and the exhaled white mist condensed into frost on the eyepiece. He cowered around the corner of the trench and listened to the distant sound of shelling, the rumbling sound, somehow, reminded him of the waterfall in his hometown...... Three months ago, he was fishing in the ice on the shores of Lake Baikal, but now he is huddled in the frozen soil of the highlands, which have been plowed countless times by the guns of the four countries, and he is tormented like hell.

"Rookie! Raise your gun high! "The stubble-faced platoon commander smashed Ivan's bulletproof vest with the butt of his rifle. The steel inserts hurt his ribs, and Ivan hurriedly raised the short assault rifle, and the condensed ice crystals on the barrel fell. Through the blackened snow, he saw a German Leopard tank engaged in a fierce exchange of fire with a Japanese Type 97 tank on the ridgeline 500 meters away...... I don't know which country's air raids left the craters, and there are still dark green oil stains.

Suddenly the radio burst out in shrill Russian: "Three o'clock direction!" Afghan maniac with RPG! Before Ivan could react, the trench he was in suddenly turned black - the dust kicked up by the rockets obscured the sky, and the cans and bullet casings that had been scattered on the ground flew around like pieces on an overturned chessboard. Suddenly, he felt some warm liquid spill into his neckline, and when he turned his head, it was the brain of Anthony, a veteran who had taught him to load magazines half an hour earlier. I saw that only half of Anthony's body was hanging from the sandbag, and the other half was gone. His intestines were steaming hot like thawed fish entrails, standing out in the gray-black dirt.

"Shoot! Shoot! The platoon commander's roar was mixed with the roar of a 12.7mm heavy machine gun. Ivan mechanically pulled the trigger. As the 5.45mm bullet passed through the falling snowflakes, the turbaned figure three hundred meters away exploded with blood in his chest. The man was killed instantly, but the bazooka in his hand was still launched, only to miss a lot, and smashed on an oil drum with the "Made in America" logo that had been left on the battlefield at some point, causing hundreds of more pieces of iron to the ground.

As night fell, Ivan huddled in a concrete bunker left behind by the Germans. The crack in the ventilation duct seeped into the minus 10 degrees Celsius cold, and the silence around him was enough to make him scared... He suddenly felt the slightly sharp bronze cross in his trouser pocket, which had been picked up from a blown up transport truck this morning, and its edges were covered with burn marks, and he felt a sense of silence as he looked at the small object that was faintly glowing with reddish-purple light.

At three o'clock in the morning, the shelling tore the night sky again. Ivan followed the assault team towards the pass, known to the Afghans as the "Valley of Blood," his boots creaking into the half-melted slush. Countless fireflies lit up in the darkness, and the Japanese Type 89 grenadiers and Russian AGS-17 grenade launchers roared at each other. At one point, Ivan saw a string of fresh footprints in the snow leading to the wreckage of a German-made Weasel armored vehicle, and he instinctively raised his gun to aim, even though he heard the cry of a newborn in the shadows — he knew that the fanatical Islamists would do anything. They use living people as bait, even babies, pregnant women, and even elderly people who have passed their old age...... Just as he was thinking, a pale-faced woman came out of the complete with the baby in her arms, and he immediately strengthened his vigilance and motioned for the other party to raise his hand. But the woman was unmoved, she smiled desolately, and pulled the safety bolt from her body with lightning speed, and Ivan now understood that it was too late. Blood flowers burst out of the woman's body, along with the high explosives strapped to her body. The last thing Ivan's consciousness remembered before falling into darkness was the shape of her mouth, even though he didn't know the Afghan language:

title: No Time to Waste
desc:
In the Ministry of Finance office in the capital, stacks of unusually tall financial reports caught the Minister of Economy's attention. Unlike usual, these reports, without exception, concerned local financial difficulties due to tax resistance:
In Nizhny Tagil, workers seized control of the arms factory, demanding an 'end to their exploitation through taxes'; in Barnaul, angry peasants used farm tools to drive away officials who came to collect grain taxes; in Magadan, merchants engaged in overseas trade formed a joint chamber of commerce, threatening the government to lower business taxes, or else they would resort to strikes and market closures.
Though mentally prepared, these reports still threw Volpin and his team into a flurry of activity. As an economist, he was well aware of the deep-seated economic ailments of his homeland. The originally long-term, moderate reform plan was now precarious due to this crisis. But if a decisive and thorough tax reform was not carried out now, the nation's financial situation would face an unprecedented crisis.
Indeed, he also knew that any reform would touch upon someone's interests, and voices of opposition would only increase. Thus, Volpin found himself in a dilemma: on one hand, the myriad citizens of the motherland had long suffered under burdensome tax policies, and rashly reducing their taxes might lead to the collapse of the financial system; on the other hand, the high-income groups in the country would undoubtedly try every means to resist paying taxes, and rashly increasing their taxes would certainly invite their counterattacks and retaliation...
Time ticked by, second by second. Volpin could no longer hear the commotion in the office. His gaze fell upon the uneven and teetering scales on his desk. [RUS.GetName]'s financial system was slowing towards the abyss of collapse. He had to...
And immediately, he made his final decision:

title: The Sin of Greed
desc:
Mr. Barannikov sat limply in the defendant's dock, his brow furrowed, a hint of unease in his eyes. The atmosphere in the courtroom was tense and solemn; the gazes of the judge and jury were all focused on him. Unlike usual, he wasn't wearing his dark suit; due to his hasty journey, he only had time to put on a shirt. He didn't look as vibrant as he usually did on television and in newspapers; his eyes were full of exhaustion.
“Court is now in session…”
Now, his palms were slightly sweaty from nervousness. The lawyer he had hired at great expense stood beside him, his voice firm and powerful, defending him. Barannikov listened to the lawyer's statement, feeling anxious. His Gaikin Group had supplied [RUS.GetName] with countless armaments, and of course, he had amassed immeasurable wealth. However, the implementation of the new tax policy was attempting to make him surrender his wealth, but for him, a man誰 money, this was absolutely impossible.
“The defendant, Gaikin Group, by exploiting multiple tax loopholes…”
He began to seek various methods to evade it all. For this, he hired the best tax consultants, attempting to protect his assets. But no matter what, all efforts seemed futile—in the end, he still found himself in the defendant's dock.
“Mr. Barannikov…”
The judge's questions were sharp and direct. Barannikov hesitated somewhat in his answers. His voice was low, occasionally stuttering due to nervousness. He had to avoid the judge's sharp gaze to find some inner peace.
Outside the court, reporters gathered at the entrance, their camera flashes constantly flickering, trying to uncover all the details of this case that could arguably decide the future of the Republic. Inside, the spectators were also whispering, exchanging their views. As the trial proceeded, his mood grew heavier. He knew the chances of winning this silent war against the tax bureau were slim. A flicker of hesitation crossed his eyes, but it was quickly replaced by a determined expression. He still hoped, no, he *had* to find a glimmer of hope, absolutely could not let these scoundrels touch his property, absolutely not…
“Silence!”
Evidence continued to be presented, his hopes gradually shattering, his sanity slowly eroding—his property, his everything. From the expressions of the judge and jury, he knew it was irreparable. Barannikov's mood shifted from nervousness to despair, followed by endless rage. He could bear it no longer, stood up and shouted, like a monkey performing an impromptu act:
“I’ve done so damn much for this country, damn it, how dare you treat me like this?!”
“The defendant will remain silent! Please observe court discipline.”
The bailiff pressed him back into his seat. No one paid him any attention; everyone tensely awaited the final result:
“It’s all over…”
They covered their faces and wept, crying out loud. The snowflakes they had created in the old era now roared and charged at them. The last shred of hope was extinguished with the judge's verdict.
“The sentence is hereby pronounced…”
“The court upholds the decision of the tax bureau. After the establishment of the Gaikin Group, Barannikov, through tax loopholes, allowed the Gaikin Group to evade billions in taxes, causing immeasurable losses to [RUS.GetName] and society. Therefore, the Gaikin Group must pay back taxes of approximately 1.3 billion rubles and a fine of approximately 700 million rubles, all to be paid in full within six months…”

title: After the Dark Night...
desc:
Before the tax cuts, Andrei's life was full of hardship. Every day, he toiled in the coal mine, sweat soaking his work clothes. His face always wore a look of fatigue, his eyes revealing a helplessness towards life. His wages barely maintained his family's basic living, and the heavy tax burden made him feel suffocated.
“How come the tax has gone up again?” Andrei complained at dinner, a hint of anxiety in his voice. His wife, Maria, listened silently, a worried look on her face. Their child, little Ivan, looked at them curiously, not understanding why his parents were always troubled by money. Andrei's brow was tightly furrowed, his eyes filled with worry about the future.
Their meals were always simple; an occasional piece of meat was a luxury. Andrei's shoes were long worn out, but he couldn't bear to buy new ones. Maria's clothes were always the same few, washed anúncios. Though life was simple, the high taxes always hung over their hearts, constantly extinguishing any warmth, suffocating them.
Later, Andrei decided to join the tax resistance protests, hoping to change the situation through collective strength. On the day of the protest, he stood among the crowd, holding a banner, shouting slogans loudly. His eyes were determined, his voice full of hope.
“We can't live like this anymore!” Andrei shouted, his voice echoing through the crowd. The loud voices spread like waves through the crowd, superimposing, eventually permeating the streets and alleys of Krasnoyarsk. At that moment, he felt an unprecedented strength, as if his voice could change the world. He felt his body filled with vitality, his heartbeat rising and falling with the waves. He felt he was no longer an ordinary coal miner, but a warrior fighting for justice and the future.
After several tax resistance protests, the government finally decided to implement tax cuts for ordinary people. The day the news arrived, Andrei was working in the coal mine. When he heard the news, he could hardly believe his ears.
“Really? Are the taxes really going down?” he asked his colleague excitedly, tears welling in his eyes. His voice trembled, but it was full of joy. His colleagues also responded excitedly; this was the fruit of their victory.
Now, Andrei's life has undergone a tremendous change. He no longer needs to work overtime to pay taxes, and life is no longer as constrained as before due to high taxes. The improvement in quality of life also allows him more time and energy to spend with his family.
“Look, Maria, we can finally buy Ivan the toy he’s always wanted,” Andrei said excitedly, holding his newly received wages, his voice full of happiness. Maria smiled at him, tears also welling in her eyes.
On the first weekend after the tax cuts, Andrei's family went for a picnic in the park early in the morning. Watching Ivan run on the grass, a long-lost smile reappeared on the couple's faces.
“Dad, look, I caught a butterfly!” Ivan ran over excitedly, holding a colorful butterfly in his hand. Andrei and Maria looked at him, this little fellow filling their hearts with pride and happiness. Their smiles were so radiant, so sincere, as if all their troubles had vanished into thin air.
Countless families like Andrei's were also enjoying this hard-earned leisure. The morning sunlight shone on their faces. Life, though not as beautiful as they had imagined, would never again be as laborious and tiring as before.

title: The Storm Abates, For Now
desc:
Inside the office, the lights were dim, only the faint glow from computer screens illuminated the room. To get [RUS.GetName]'s finances back on track as soon as possible, the Minister of Economy and his team had been working continuously for weeks. Everyone looked exhausted, but no one dared to slacken their efforts in the slightest.
The tables were piled high with documents and coffee cups. A map of Russia hung on the wall, with financially distressed regions marked in red. Outside, the night view of Moscow appeared exceptionally tranquil in the darkness. Pedestrians walked by rustling softly, completely unaware of the intense work underway in the nearby office.
Long nights had left dark circles under the Minister's eyes. Though weary, his gaze remained firm. He understood that if they did not fight these difficulties to the death, only endless depression awaited the motherland.
“Minister!” A startled cry suddenly rang out in the office. “Magadan’s report has finally been submitted! Their financial system can finally operate normally this month.”
“We did it,” the Minister’s voice was hoarse, but joy was still evident. “Our reform measures are starting to take effect.”
He felt an unprecedented sense of accomplishment, but soon, a deep weariness washed over him again. He knew this was just the beginning; they still had a long way to go. Cheers erupted in the office; they knew what this report meant.
The Minister crossed off the last red circle on the map. Looking at the densely crossed-out red circles, thinking of how those wealthy merchants and dignitaries had finally shut their mouths, he now had enough funds for the next step of reform.
“Have Magadan and other places recompile new financial reports and send them over. We need more precise data to guide our decisions,” the Minister emphasized. “We must ensure our reforms not only solve current problems but also lay a solid foundation for future development.”
“We cannot stop here,” the Minister murmured. “The foundations of tax reform are still not solid enough. We need to keep moving forward, until we achieve final victory.”
After a moment of silence, the Minister took out the tax reform plan that had been idle for some time. Although it had once been nearly scrapped due to this crisis, after much mending and patching, it was now ready to be reactivated.
“Get [RUS.GetLeader] on the phone,” the Minister said. “Now we have to roll up our sleeves and give this country a resounding revolution.”

title: [RUS.GetName] Tax Reduction Act
desc:
Act Number: Republic Tax Law XXXX-XX
Submission Date: Month XX, XXXX
Submitting Body: Ministry of Finance of [RUS.GetName]
Primary Drafter: Volnin
Introduction
Given the current economic situation and the tax burden on citizens, the government of [RUS.GetName] has decided to formally implement tax reduction measures through legislation to stimulate economic growth, improve people's living standards, and optimize the tax structure. This act aims to reduce the tax burden on low- and middle-income groups while ensuring the stability of national finances.
Chapter One: Tax Reduction Goals and Principles
1. Goals:
Alleviate the tax burden on low- and middle-income families.
Promote consumption and stimulate economic growth.
Enhance the fairness and transparency of the tax system.
2. Principles:
Fairness: Ensure the tax burden is fairly distributed among all social strata.
Transparency: Simplify tax laws and improve the transparency of tax policies.
Sustainability: Ensure the long-term viability of tax policies without undermining national fiscal stability.
Chapter Two: Tax Reduction Measures
…………
Chapter Three: Implementation and Supervision
…………
Chapter Four: Supplementary Provisions
1. Legal Effect:
In case of conflict between this act and existing tax laws, this act shall prevail.
The right to interpret this act belongs to the Ministry of Finance of [RUS.GetName].
2. Amendment and Repeal:
This act may be amended or repealed by a decision of the State Duma based on economic development and fiscal needs.

title: The River of Funds Flows On...
desc:
Syktyvkar, during the years of the Komi Republic, was filled with violence, conspiracy, and madness. But now, it bathes in the morning sun. On the streets, people are burying the traces of Pandora's Box in the ruins of the past. As funds from [RUS.GetName] begin to flow into this war-torn city, people are dismantling the ubiquitous armories and fortifications along the streets, hope and determination re-emerging on their faces. In the future, Syktyvkar may not become Russia's most beautiful or prosperous city, but it will certainly not be like the city of the past.
Omsk was almost entirely destroyed during the war, but it is now undergoing tremendous changes. Investment from [RUS.GetName] has not only greatly improved the city's appearance but also brought new industrial projects. The intense desire for revenge that once permeated the city is gradually fading. Thick black smoke once again billows from factory chimneys, and the roar of machinery proclaims the city's future to the heavens. Omsk's industrial heart is beating again, but unlike before, it no longer produces only guns and weapons for slaughter, but also rye bread to benefit the masses.
Tomsk, long neglected, is now ushering in its spring. Investment from [RUS.GetName] has allowed the city's cultural potential to be fully realized. In the city center, new buildings are rising one after another. Workers, free from tax burdens, labor diligently on construction sites. The roar of machinery intertwines with people's laughter, forming a harmonious symphony. Along the streets, newly planted trees are beginning to sprout tender green leaves, allowing this gray city to regain its true colors. Museums, libraries, and art centers, long unmaintained, have been revitalized, attracting tourists and scholars from all over the country. Though traces of the Central Siberian Republic are hard to find, Tomsk's cultural light is beginning to illuminate all of Russia.
Petropavlovsk, a port city once overlooked due to its remote location and the departure of the Red Navy, has now finally caught the attention of the [RUS.GetName] government, which intends to develop it into Russia's new trade center and important naval port after Magadan. Large sums of money have repaired the facilities of the abandoned port, attracting ships and merchants from all over the world. On the port's docks, goods from the OFN, and even Japan and Germany, are piled high, with merchants busily trading. Not far away, the Pacific Fleet at the Petropavlovsk naval base is conducting exercises in full swing, preparing thoroughly for future contingencies. Perhaps people should believe that this once almost desolate city does not belong to pristine nature.

title: Banners on the Dnieper
desc:
The air in Kyiv was thick with dust, smoke, and a peculiar silence—the silence that falls when artillery has just ceased, and the living dare not yet speak loudly. Ivan leaned against the shell-pocked wreck of a BTR, wearily watching the grey sky. They had done it. From the frozen north, they had pushed south, across battlefields strewn with corpses, and now the banner representing a unified Russia finally flew over this ancient city. The radio repeatedly broadcast news of victory, proclaiming that the Ukrainian people had been liberated from 'forty years of brutal fascist bandit rule' and returned to the 'embrace of the great Slavic family.'

Sounded grandiose, Ivan thought. Just like something those political department types, who’d never smelled gunpowder, would write. But what he saw before him was far removed from the radio’s fervent paeans. No welcoming crowds with food and drink, no cheering throngs. Only faces, sallow and hollow-eyed, cautiously peering out from basements and crevices in the ruins. No joy on their faces, more like numbness, doubt, and a weariness that cut to the bone. They eyed Ivan and his comrades as they would a pack of bears that had just driven off wolves but might themselves be devourer.

Yesterday, Ivan’s squad, while clearing remnants of the enemy in a half-demolished apartment building, had found an old woman hiding in a closet. She clutched a faded, strangely embroidered cloth bundle, muttering to herself in a language he almost couldn't understand, yet found vaguely familiar. Not German, not Russian. When the soldiers tried to pull her out, she fast raised her head, a nearly extinguished spark in her cloudy eyes, and said in a hoarse but startlingly clear voice: “We are Ukrainians.”

Just that one sentence. No thanks, no accusations, just a statement so simple it was almost stubborn. As if reminding them, and herself, that after the oppression of Germanization, the endless grain requisitions, the terror of the secret police, and the daily humiliations, some things, like tenacious grassroots under the black earth, had not died. Ivan had later seen hand-drawn trident symbols hidden in wall cracks in cleared houses, heard fragments of sad, off-key songs drifting from some window at night, their melodies definitely not from Moscow.

They had been ruled for forty years. Forty years, long enough for a generation to be born, grow up, and grow old. Their cities were renamed, their language forbidden in official use, their history altered or erased. Children were forced to learn German, singing songs praising another “Führer.” Wheat from the black earth was ceaselessly shipped to Germania, while locals often struggled on the brink of starvation. Ivan recalled reading about the “Holodomor” in history books, a tragedy of another era, but for many elderly people here, perhaps it was just a repetition in a different form.

Now, they were “liberated.” Tanks rolled over squares once adorned with swastikas; new portraits replaced old ones. But looking at those silent, complex-eyed Ukrainians, Ivan suddenly felt a wave of confusion. How should history be remembered? Whose sacrifices should be eulogized? Whose suffering should be recounted? The memories carried by this land were far heavier, far more complex, than they had initially imagined. They had brought back the banner, but could they truly bring back those souls suppressed, distorted, and whispered about in the long, dark night?

Ivan sighed and re-shouldered his rifle. At least, the fighting was over. At least, they had come.

title: The First Brick on the Ruins
desc:
The morning mist had not yet dispersed, and sunlight struggled to penetrate the dust lingering over Kyiv, falling on the pitted cobblestones of Saint Andrew's Descent. The air was a mixture of damp earth, lime, and an indescribable scent of new beginnings. Once, this place echoed with the rhythmic tread of marching boots, sharp German commands, and occasional gunshots. Now, a different kind of symphony had taken its place—the clang of hammers striking stone, the rough chants of porters, the creak of temporary scaffolding, and... the whisper of hope.

“Comrades, put your backs into it! This wall must be finished before nightfall!” shouted a foreman wearing an old, mortar-stained military cap, his voice booming. Beneath his feet lay a scene of devastation—collapsed walls, charred beams, scattered rubble. Just a few months ago, this was a battlefield. Now, it was a construction site. Men, mostly elderly veterans or young men who had just laid down their rifles, labored in silence and with focus. They passed bricks, mixed mortar, their movements clumsy yet imbued with an almost stubborn determination. Each brick laid seemed to declare to the dark past: We are back, and we will reclaim our home.

Not far away, several women were painstakingly clearing debris with wicker baskets, their headscarves covering half their faces, revealing only eyes that were weary yet resilient. As they cleared, they spoke in low voices, an occasional suppressed sob heard, but more often, whispers of mutual encouragement. “Soon, Alyona, a few more baskets and we’ll see the foundation.” “Careful, Tamara, that stone isn’t stable.” They were clearing not just rubble, but the fragments of life buried by war—broken pottery, charred picture frames, rusted farm tools... Each item silently told a story forcibly interrupted.

Occasionally, Russian soldiers in uniform would patrol by, their gazes sweeping over the busy crowd, their expressions complex. Some would stop, awkwardly helping to move a few bricks, earning a few heavily accented “thank yous.” Others merely watched in silence, as if contemplating the meaning of this reconstruction and their role in this land. The air was no longer filled with hostility, but with a cautious coexistence, a fragile understanding built upon common ruins.

In the distance, the Dnieper River flowed silently on, reflecting the gradually brightening sky and the city’s battered skyline. The road to reconstruction was long, and the painful memories were far from healed. But this first brick, this first chant, this first ray of sunlight piercing the dust, was like a seed falling upon the traumatized black earth. Perhaps, as their poet wrote…

title: Seeds Beneath the Black Earth
desc:
Petro's boots sank deep into the muddy black earth, each step making a dull squelch. The air mixed the dampness of the early spring thaw with an indescribable smell of rusted metal and decaying bones. Was this the granary they promised? This fabled land where a walking stick planted would supposedly sprout? He looked around; the fields were pockmarked with craters, like a face ravaged by smallpox. On the distant horizon, the twisted silhouette of a derelict tank stabbed at the leaden sky, a monument left from the last liberation, or perhaps the one before that? Who could even remember.

Instructors from the city, in their clean uniforms, generously distributed seeds—small, shriveled grains in sacks الناس by faded, illegible Cyrillic letters. They patted Petro's shoulder, speaking passionately about 'Five-Year Plans,' 'agricultural modernization,' and 'contributing grain to the great motherland.' Petro just nodded, forcing a look of requisite gratitude and enthusiasm. He didn't tell the instructor that last autumn, in this very field, he had dug up an unexploded German aerial bomb that nearly sent his whole family to meet Hrut. Nor did he mention that the previous rulers had also promised tractors, only to deliver a pile of rusty parts and an incomprehensible German manual.

Neighbor Ivan squatted at the edge of the field, rolling a cheap makhorka cigarette, watching Petro struggle with his ancestral, endlessly repaired wooden plow. “Petro,” Ivan exhaled a thick cloud of smoke, his voice like sandpaper, “they say this black earth has a spirit; it knows what you plant. Do you think it knows whether we’re planting hope now, or another crop of suffering?”

Petro stopped, wiped the sweat from his brow, a mixture of soil and perspiration. “Who knows, Ivan,” he panted, “Maybe it only knows hunger. It’s been hungry for decades, and we’ve been hungry for decades. Now, someone says let us feed it, and then it will feed us. Sounds… fair.” His tone carried an almost numb sense of fatalism. Fair? On this land, 'fair' was a luxury.

He bent down, grabbed a handful of seeds from the cloth bag, the shriveled grains pricking his calloused palm. He looked at this land,hit countless times, a land that had devoured corpses, drunk blood, and borne too many broken promises. Unified. Yes, no more men in different uniforms shooting at each other here. That was progress, undoubtedly. Life was perhaps a little better, like the air by a winter fire, slightly warmer. But this land… it was so tired.

Petro took a deep breath and scattered the seeds onto the turned earth. Black grains fell on black soil, silently. Would they sprout? Would they bear fruit? Or would they be washed away by the coming rains, or pecked clean by crows? No one knew. But he scattered the seeds anyway, because what else could he do? This was his land, no matter how much pain it carried.

title: Signed, Sealed, Can't Read It
desc:
Summer had barely settled in when a new face appeared in the village—a young man with thick glasses and a neat but slightly countrified uniform, calling himself a 'Land Relations Coordinator' sent from the district. He brought several stacks of brand-new documents reeking of ink, and an enthusiasm that sent a chill down Petro's spine. The coordinator gathered the villagers in front of the dilapidated village office, gushing about the new 'land to the tiller' policy, words hailing down on Petro's muddled head like hailstones: 'cadastral registration,' 'land use certificates,' 'collective responsibility linked to individual profit'...
Petro was handed a stiff piece of paper, covered in dense Cyrillic script, and a bright red stamp depicting what looked like some kind of fierce bird. He looked at it sideways, then upright, brought it close to his eyes, then held it up to the sunlight, squinting. The letters danced before him like a swarm of drunken ants, performing an incomprehensible ballet. His rough fingers traced the paper's edge. This thing was thicker than a ration coupon, but far less substantial than a good scythe.
“Petro Ivanovich!” The young coordinator clapped him on the shoulder, his smile as bright as the red star on Moscow's square. “Congratulations! Look! This piece of land, from now on, it belongs to you! Well, strictly speaking, it’s a long-term stable use right, but practically, it’s yours! Work hard for the great motherland!”
“Mine?” Petro repeated numbly, his voice sounding like it came from a dry well. “What d’you mean? This land… hasn’t it always been me farming it? My pa farmed it, my grandpappy too. It was this piece when the Germans came, and this piece when the last liberators came. How’s it become mine now?” He pointed to the familiar patch of black earth nearby, just starting to show some green shoots. “Does this stamp on this paper make the stones in the field run away by themselves? Or will next year’s rain listen to my commands?”
Old Ivan, puffing on his pipe nearby, muttered, “Careful, Petro. The Tsar used to say the land was his, then the commissar said the land was collective, now they say the land is yours. This land, eh, it’s like a disobedient wife. Nobody’s word counts, only God Almighty’s and your own strength.”
Petro ignored Ivan's grumbling. He looked down at the 'certificate' again, trying to find some familiar trace in those twisted symbols—perhaps 'potato'? Or 'tax'? Nothing. He only recognized his own name, Petro Ivanovich, clumsily printed at the top. He suddenly felt a dizzying sense of absurdity. This land, soaked with the sweat, and occasionally the blood, of generations of his family, was now 'his' because of a piece of paper he couldn't read?
He looked up at the black field, the early summer wind carrying the scent of earth and grass. The land was still the same land, silent and stoic. Slowly, carefully, he folded the stiff paper and tucked it into the worn pocket of his shirt, right next to his heart. There, the paper's edges pressed against his skin through the coarse cloth. An unprecedented emotion, a mixture of immense confusion and a tiny, almost negligible… perhaps… hope? stirred in his numb heart like a newly sprouted seedling.
Wow… he really had land? Even if only a piece of paper he couldn't make heads or tails of said so.

title: The New 'Cooperative' Neighbors
desc:
The 'land certificate' had barely warmed in Petro's breast pocket when new developments arrived in the village. This time, it wasn't an enthusiastic young man, but a stern-faced, middle-aged man who spoke with a thick bureaucratic accent. His uniform collar was stiffer than the most presentable tablecloth in Petro's house. He summoned all the villagers who had received 'certificates' and announced a grand initiative called the 'Agricultural Production Cooperative Pilot Program.'
“Comrades!” His voice echoed in the empty village hall, carrying an undeniable authority. “Individual farming is inefficient and cannot bear the heavy responsibility of revitalizing the motherland's granary! To increase output, share resources, and concentrate efforts on major tasks, we have decided to establish agricultural cooperatives! Everyone's land, tools, and even that lame old horse,” he pointed to old Ivan's animal tied to a tree, “will be uniformly managed by the cooperative, with distribution according to labor, more work means more reward!”
Petro stood in the crowd, scratching his scalp vigorously, trying to make sense of the tongue-twisting words. Uniform management? Distribution according to labor? This sounded… awfully familiar. He remembered as a child, another group of men in different uniforms had said similar things, only then it was called a 'collective farm.' Then too, they talked about 'concentrating efforts.' And the result? The grain was indeed concentrated, but it all ended up on the grain requisition teams' trucks.
“What?” Old Ivan was the first to jump up, his pipe almost falling to the ground. “My old horse may be lame, but it's mine! Why should it be uniformly managed by you? I ask you, if I want to leave a couple of potatoes for my grandson, do I have to submit a report?”
The middle-aged official pushed up his glasses, his face impassive. “Comrade Ivan Stepanovich, this is for the common good. The cooperative will uniformly provide seeds, fertilizer, and coordinate plowing times. At the end ofthe year, income will be calculated based on work points, ensuring fairness and justice, and you'll also get priority access to state-supplied agricultural machinery.” He paused, his tone becoming more emphatic. “Of course, we won't force comrades who are unwilling to join. It's just that… farmers outside the cooperative, in terms of resource allocation and agricultural product procurement prices, may… experience some differences.”

The rationed flour, though unpalatable, was at least enough; the village road had been repaired, still a dirt road, but with fewer potholes; most importantly, he could sleep soundly at night. But… his stomach did feel a bit fuller than before. He sighed heavily and, like the other villagers, pressed his fingerprint onto another document he couldn't understand.

This time, it wasn't an enthusiastic young man, but a stern-faced, middle-aged man who spoke with a thick bureaucratic accent. His uniform collar was stiffer than the most presentable tablecloth in Petro's house. He summoned all the villagers who had received 'certificates' and announced a grand initiative called the 'Agricultural Production Cooperative Pilot Program.'

title: Divided Land, Familiar Taste
desc:
Mikhail, shouldering his oft-repaired old plow, trudged through the tilled black earth. The scent of spring finally overpowered the muddy odor of melting snow, carrying a faint, elusive fragrance of grass. Unlike previous years, the land beneath his feet, according to the red-headed document posted on the wall of the village cooperative, was now 'clearly allocated' for his family to cultivate. Of course, the lion's share of the harvest still had to go to the state, but at least, nominally, they had 'their own' land, instead of relying on the heavens and the whims of cadres for their yearly allotment.
His son, little Vasya, now almost as tall as Mikhail's shoulder, was no longer the little tyke who only knew to ask, 'Is life getting better?' He awkwardly followed his father, learning to sow a high-yield potato seed, supposedly 'scientifically cultivated.' The boy's strength had grown, and he could help quite a bit, though his movements were still clumsy, scattering seeds unevenly.
“Dad,” Vasya panted, wiping sweat from his brow, “Uncle Yakov from the cooperative said if the harvest is good this year, we can get two extra bags of potatoes! Is it true?”
Mikhail straightened up,shock his aching back, and gazed at this endless stretch of his own land. “That’s what the paper says, son.” He paused, spat. “Whether we get it in hand, well, that depends on whether God—oh no, whether Comrade Lenin’s spirit in heaven blesses us, and also on whether that fat political commissar who collects the grain is in a good mood.”
Yes, there were changes. The village loudspeaker no longer blared wartime songs daily but started promoting the benefits of 'agricultural cooperation,' saying everyone was now the master of the land. The soup in the canteen was a little thicker, occasionally with a few specks of oil. A small shop had opened in town; though its shelves were mostly empty, at least there was the idea of it.
But Mikhail knew in his heart, this land was still the same land, the soil still the same soil. What to plant, how to plant it, was mostly decided from above. How much grain to hand over, how much to keep, were iron-clad regulations. The so-called 'reward for labor' was more like the few potatoes he used to secretly pocket, now allowed to be pocketed openly—provided, of course, you first completed your delivery quota.
He watched his son scatter seeds with an excitement, an almost faith-like fervor, and his heart was a mix of emotions. Perhaps for the young, this was hope? A tangible, visible hope, even if it was only a thin layer. Well, having hope was better than having none.
Mikhail gripped the plow handles again and shouted, “Put your back into it, boy! We have to finish this furrow before dark! Otherwise, there’ll be no potato pancakes for you at dinner!”

title: Smoke Rings by the Dnieper
desc:
The Kyiv dusk carried a scent of steel and dust, the setting sun struggling to paint the Dnieper golden, only to be sharply fragmented by the stark silhouettes of new Russian-style apartment buildings. Oleg sat at the wobbly table in his kitchen, a half-empty, almost label-less bottle of vodka and a saucer of darkly pickled cucumbers before him. His son, seventeen-year-old Sasha, was hunched over a brand-new history textbook, its pages exuding the smell of cheap ink.
“Dad,” Sasha’s voice was hesitant, breaking the silence, “the book says… we are all an indivisible part of the great Russian nation, and past sufferings were due to separatist plots and foreign powers…” He looked up, his young face etched with confusion. “But Grandma always told me we were descendants of Cossacks, singing songs of Kyivan Rus…”
Oleg didn’t answer immediately, just poured himself a full glass of vodka and downed it, a satisfied yet bitter gurgle sounding in his throat. He rolled a coarse makhorka cigarette, lit it with a match, and took a deep drag, the smoke blurring his weather-beaten face. “Books,” he finally spoke, his voice hoarse, “books are written by victors, Sasha. Like bread distributed from the ration station—they give you what they give, and you eat it, whether it tastes like sawdust mixed with mud or not.”
“But the teacher said national unity is the top priority, to forget past unpleasantness to build a strong new motherland…”
“Build a motherland?” Oleg scoffed, ash falling onto his patched trousers. “We’ve been building motherlands all our lives. First, building for some mustachioed madman in the Polish mud, then ‘building’ for those waving tridents and shouting slogans in the ruins of Crimea, then later building for some big-bearded general in the rubble of Kharkiv… Now, we’re to build for the comrades from Moscow. Every construction means tearing down something old, forgetting some old names. They say it’s for unity, for strength.” He gestured out the window. “Look at that new Comrade Street. It used to be called Khreshchatyk. Your grandma used to take me there to buy Easter eggs. Now, there are only grey concrete slabs and uniform slogans.”
Sasha fell silent, his fingers unconsciously stroking the portrait of a leader he’d never seen, printed on the book’s page. “Then… what… what are we?” the boy asked softly, a question that seemed to have troubled him for a long time.
Oleg stubbed out his cigarette and lit another. He didn’t look at Sasha but gazed at the murky waters of the Dnieper. “What are we?” he repeated, his voice dropping. “We are people who plant potatoes, who drink vodka to keep warm, who secretly sing the songs of our ancestors in our hearts. We are people who remember Khreshchatyk Street. We are people who have watched flags change again and again, yet still survive on this black earth.”
He turned, his gaze fixing on his son, sharp as a tack. “Listen, Sasha,” he said, tapping his own chest with a rough finger, then pointing to Sasha, “the blood in your veins comes from this land. The first words you spoke were in the Kyiv accent. Never, ever forget that. Even if the whole world forgets, you yourself cannot forget. You are Ukrainian.”
The father and son remained silent for a long time. Outside, the sky had completely darkened, only scattered lights twinkling on the far bank of the Dnieper. Oleg picked up the cigarette pack from the table and offered one to Sasha. Sasha hesitated, then took it. Two crimson embers glowed in the dim kitchen, smoke curling, filling the silence.

title: Katyusha and Quotas
desc:
When Sasha returned from school, he saw a new, almost garishly colored poster pasted at the alley entrance. It depicted a buxom, robust Ukrainian mother with a standard smile, cradling three equally rosy-cheeked infants, against a backdrop of rolling wheat fields and towering factory chimneys. A huge slogan in bold Cyrillic letters read: “Hero Mothers—The Pride and Future of the Motherland!” Smaller text detailed the latest reward policy for families with three or more children—some extra cloth coupons, and perhaps priority in purchasing low-quality candies.
At dinner, the kitchen was filled with the bland smell of boiled cabbage. Sasha, absentmindedly poking at the potato chunks in his bowl, finally spoke up: “Dad, they put up new posters in the street, saying it’s glorious to have many children, that it’s a contribution to the country… The teacher also said we have too few people, the Germans, the Americans, they have many…”
Oleg, struggling to cut a hard loaf of black bread with a dull knife, paused. He picked up the half-empty vodka bottle from the table and poured himself another glass, the murky liquid sloshing. “Glorious,” he snorted, gulping down the alcohol. “Yes, glorious. As glorious as the collective farm tractors back then. They need manpower, Sasha. They need workers to fill the factories, soldiers to fill the barracks, enough people to shout ‘Hurrah!’ and wave flags.”
He twisted a cigarette butt between his fingers. “Your grandmother’s generation, she had seven, three survived. No one called it glorious then, only hard-fated, said they couldn’t raise them. Now they want your mother, want Marsha from next door, to pop out babies like chicks from eggs. Glorious? Those cloth coupons they give, are they enough to make diapers for a newborn? Enough to buy a sip of milk? They draw you a big pie flying in the sky and then make you chase it on an empty stomach.”
Oleg lit his cigarette, took a deep drag, smoke curling. “They say we’re not the womb of Europe. Sounds nice. But they want women to open their wombs, one after another, how is that different from a sow farrowing? Marsha is only in her early thirties, looks older than your grandmother. Her man? Died two years ago in a ‘peacekeeping mission,’ on some godforsaken border, couldn’t even find his bones. Now she’s raising five kids alone, by washing clothes for officers in exchange for some potatoes. Glorious? Bullshit glorious.”
He flicked his ash. “The country needs a future, Sasha. But a future isn’t born from quotas and slogans. It’s nurtured by hot soup, by warm boots, by being able to sleep soundly at night. Don’t believe those posters, kid. The wheat in the posters can’t be eaten, the children in the posters don’t cry.”
Sasha fell silent, looking down at the few lonely potatoes in his bowl. Outside the kitchen window, the night grew darker, and the distant factory chimneys continued to spew black smoke tirelessly into the boundless twilight.

title: Golden Ears in Black Earth
desc:
It was time again to sell grain to the state. Oleg stood by the dusty threshing floor, watching sack after sack of plump wheat being loaded onto creaking trucks. Under the sun, the golden ears of wheat piled up like mountains, dazzling the eyes. On the radio, a broadcaster with a sonorous, perfectly enunciated voice, was passionately announcing: “…Ukraine, the granary of our great motherland, has once again over-fulfilled its aid mission to the fraternal European nations! The fertile black earth has once again proven the superiority of the system! Golden waves of wheat will nourish the entire progressive world…”
Sasha was also nearby, helping to carry sacks, sweat soaking his thin shirt. He stopped to catch his breath, wiped the sweat and dust from his face, and walked over to his father. “Dad, we’ve harvested so much grain, we really are the ‘granary of Europe’!” His young face bore a trace of pride, similar to the broadcaster’s, infected by the grand narrative.
Oleg spat out the blade of grass he was chewing, his eyes complex as he watched the departing trucks laden with grain. “Yes, a granary. Someone else’s granary.” He pulled a crumpled cigarette pack from his pocket, took one out, and lit it. “Look at this wheat, Sasha, golden and beautiful. Know where it’s going? To Moscow, to Warsaw, to Prague, to Berlin—God knows where else. It’ll become decent white bread for those city folks, a garnish on their tables.”
“But we’re helping fraternal nations, Dad. The book says this is internationalism…”
“Internationalism?” Oleg let out a dry laugh, smoke escaping from between his teeth. “Yes, great internationalism. It means tightening your belt, taking the life-sustaining grain you dug out of your fields, and loading it onto trains for ‘brothers’ thousands of versts away, whose names you don’t even know. Then they give you a few certificates, call you a ‘labor model,’ and give you a few empty promises, saying tractors will arrive in the village next year—year after year.”
He pointed to their meager private plot. “What about our own land? After handing over the public grain each year, what’s left is barely enough to get us through to spring. Your mother still has to find ways to mix potatoes with flour to make bread. We are a granary? Ha! We are sacks for others to fill with grain; once filled, they’re carried away. Who cares if the sack is torn, or if it’s hungry?”
Oleg took a harsh drag from his cigarette. “Remember, Sasha, this black earth is our mother; it can feed us. But now, it has to feed others first. When it can feed us first, before ‘aiding fraternal nations,’ then that will be truly good times. Don’t be fooled by the slogans on the loudspeakers and the numbers in the newspapers.”
The trucks kicked up a cloud of dust and drove off, leaving behind an empty threshing floor and the fragrance of wheat straw. Father and son stood there silently, watching the convoy disappear over the horizon. Oleg threw his cigarette butt to the ground, crushed it with his boot, and pulled out another from his pocket, lighting it anew.

title: Dust and Echoes on the Great Dam
desc:
Zaporizhzhia, on the banks of the Dnieper. Taras's sweat dripped onto the scorching concrete, evaporating instantly. The deafening roar—concrete mixers, pile drivers, the howl of heavy trucks—had almost become part of his life. He couldn't remember how many years it had been; like ants, they toiled on this war-ravaged land, rebuilding the massive hydroelectric power station that was once the pride of the republic, later a victim of both sides' scorched-earth policies.
New flags fluttered over the construction site, and loudspeakers blared perpetually optimistic marches and speeches by leading comrades about 'electrification illuminating the future.' Taras was already numb to it. He remembered earlier times, as a child, when his father had also worked here. Then, people's eyes shone with light, believing every stone, every bag of cement, was adding to a brighter world. Later, that light was extinguished, accompanied by deafening explosions and the Dnieper's angry roar. His father didn't live to see that day.
Now, they were back. With the same tenacious spirit, using equipment transported from 'fraternal republics' that often broke down, and with tens of thousands of rough hands like his own. The radio said this was a 'miracle of the people's will,' a 'powerful counterattack against fascist saboteurs.' Taras felt it was more like a struggle against themselves, against this unruly river, against that damned, ever-present past.
He and his fellow workers lived in temporary sheds, lit at night by dim bulbs—if they were lucky and the power was on. Watching the dam rise again day by day, like a grey scar across the river, Taras felt a strange emptiness. Where would this immense power flow? To light up Kyiv's neon nights, or to drive the gears of factories in distant borderlands? Perhaps both. But right now, he only felt the ache in his back, and the concrete dust that could never be completely washed away.

options.name: The river will always flow, no matter where.
options.text: The river will always flow, no matter where.

He couldn't remember how many years it had been; like ants, they toiled on this war-ravaged land, rebuilding the massive hydroelectric power station that was once the pride of the republic, later a victim of both sides' scorched-earth policies.
New flags fluttered over the construction site, and loudspeakers blared perpetually optimistic marches and speeches by leading comrades about 'electrification illuminating the future.' Taras was already numb to it. He remembered earlier times, as a child, when his father had also worked here. Then, people's eyes shone with light, believing every stone, every bag of cement, was adding to a brighter world. Later, that light was extinguished, accompanied by deafening explosions and the Dnieper's angry roar. His father didn't live to see that day.
Now, they were back. With the same tenacious spirit, using equipment transported from 'fraternal republics' that often broke down, and with tens of thousands of rough hands like his own. The radio said this was a 'miracle of the people's will,' a 'powerful counterattack against fascist saboteurs.' Taras felt it was more like a struggle against themselves, against this unruly river, against that damned, ever-present past.
He and his fellow workers lived in temporary sheds, lit at night by dim bulbs—if they were lucky and the power was on. Watching the dam rise again day by day, like a grey scar across the river, Taras felt a strange emptiness. Where would this immense power flow? To light up Kyiv's neon nights, or to drive the gears of factories in distant borderlands? Perhaps both. But right now, he only felt the ache in his back, and the concrete dust that could never be completely washed away.

title: Distant Bright Lights and Flickering Candles
desc:
On the outskirts of Poltava, Oksana once again skillfully tightened the base of a loose lightbulb. The dim yellow light flickered a few times and finally stabilized, barely illuminating her simple hut and the mending work spread out on the table. Outside, massive high-voltage power towers stood like steel giants, silently striding across the fields, extending thick cables towards a hazy distance—supposedly Poland, perhaps even further.
The radio was broadcasting the evening news, the announcer declaring in that distinctive, proud tone: “…This quarter’s electricity export quota has once again been over-fulfilled! Ukraine’s surging power is continuously being supplied to fraternal nations, strongly supporting the common prosperity of the Collective Security Treaty Organization…” Oksana snorted, paying no attention. She was more concerned about whether her electricity bill would go up again this month, and whether the village sawmill could operate normally tomorrow—the last power outage halted wood processing for half the village, leaving the men to grumble in the tavern.
Her neighbor, old Ivan, leaning on his cane, came in to borrow some salt. “Did you hear, Oksana? All our electricity is going abroad; Moscow must be very bright!” A hint of sarcasm touched the old man’s wizened face. “And here? Hah, our lightbulbs are like fireflies, on and off. Truly, the fat flows to outsiders’ fields.”
Oksana handed him the salt cellar and sighed: “Uncle Ivan, say less. They say this is the bigger picture, a ‘strategic necessity.’ What do we common folk understand?” But in her heart, she thought of her child doing homework at night, having to huddle under the lightbulb, unable to see the book clearly from a little further away. And those power lines, supposedly carrying “surging power,” hummed overhead, sending light to people she would never meet. This must be what it felt like to be a granary, she mused. Empty stomach, watching the grain being shipped away, and now even the light had to be shared with others.
She fiddled with the mending thread, by that unstable light. The distant power towers were silent silhouettes in the night, steadfastly fulfilling their 'internationalist duty'.

title: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
desc:
Levko stood a few hundred meters away from the massive concrete dome, feeling the ground beneath his feet vibrate slightly. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the republic's newest pride, or rather, its newest behemoth, was undergoing some critical tests. He was a young technician, transferred from Lviv, responsible for monitoring the pressure readings of the cooling system. Everything here exuded a sense of the future, and also a chilling unfamiliarity.
The site was teeming with people in white or grey uniforms, wearing badges with numbers and letters, their faces stern. Armed guards were stationed every few steps, and the barbed wire fences bore yellow and black radiation warning signs—that strange trefoil symbol, said to represent an invisible, intangible 'fire' that could kill you. Old workers privately called it the 'atomic will-o'-the-wisp.'
Levko had received training, knew all the safety procedures, and understood what the Geiger counter readings meant. But he still couldn't completely shake off a sense of awe and a tinge of fear. This was entirely different from burning coal or damming a river. What they were taming was the power of the sun's core, the secret of stellar combustion. Propaganda posters depicted atomic energy as a gentle giant, capable of providing 'inexhaustible clean energy,' able to 'illuminate the entire republic overnight.'
However, what was locked behind those clean control rooms and thick lead doors? Levko sometimes found himself staring at the silent, immense silhouette of the reactor during night shifts. It resembled a slumbering beast, its breathing steady, but you knew it could awaken at any moment and unleash devastating power. His colleagues sometimes joked that if they made an operational error, they would instantly become 'ashes of the state.' Behind the jokes lay an unspoken tension.
Today's test seemed to be going smoothly; all readings were within normal ranges. Levko signed his name in the logbook, relieved. After work, he walked out of the plant area and saw the Dnieper River glistening in the sunset, smoke curling from a village炊 on the riverbank. Everything was peaceful and serene, as if this concrete and steel giant belonged to a different world. He didn't know what this 'peaceful atom' would ultimately bring to this land. The promised light, or a hidden shadow?
He pulled a crumpled cigarette pack from his pocket, lit one, and took a deep drag. The smell of tobacco temporarily overpowered the faint, disinfectant-like 'scientific' scent in the air.
