title: The Horn Sounds from the Red Walls
desc:
The ancient red walls of the Kremlin reflected a deep, resolute light under the rising morning sun. Snow had not yet completely melted, but a hint of thaw could already be sniffed in the air. In a newly renovated hall, still smelling faintly of fresh paint, the indicator light on a radio lit up. A steady, clear voice, tinged with barely concealed weariness yet full of strength, carried through the airwaves across the vast land just emerging from war and division, even crossing borders to reach a world still reeling.

“Peoples of all Russia! Friends around the world! Brothers and sisters!”

“We have experienced a night as deep as the abyss. The iron heel of fascism trampled our homeland; the bayonet of division pierced our heart. Hunger, fear, humiliation, fratricide… these words were once the footnotes of our lives. Too many lost their homes, lost loved ones, lost hope. We once thought this great land would forever sink into darkness.”

“But!” The voice suddenly rose, carrying a long-suppressed cry. “We did not surrender! The soul of Russia is indomitable! From the frozen Arctic tundra to the rolling waves of the Don, from ravaged Smolensk to Kazan city that has seen empires rise and fall, the people never gave up! Partisan bonfires burned in the forests, factory machines roared under artillery fire, mothers fed children with their last piece of black bread, soldiers built a great wall with their flesh and blood!”

“Today, we stand here, beneath the red walls of the Kremlin, to declare to the world: the division is over! Tyranny has been overthrown! A unified Russia is reborn from the flames!”

“Yes, we are scarred and devastated. The path of reconstruction is long and arduous. But we are no longer alone, no longer divided! Cities will be rebuilt, villages will be revitalized, factories will roar again, fields will yield harvests once more! We must heal the wounds, mend the fissures, allow all people living on this land, regardless of ethnicity or faith, to enjoy peace, dignity, and sustenance!”

“We extend our hands to the world—not in supplication, but in invitation! Inviting all forces that cherish peace and oppose oppression to join us in building a better future! Let the bells of the Kremlin toll the dawn of a new era! Russia has awakened!”

Stirring music swelled from the radio, replacing the powerful voice. In distant villages, in newly reopened factories, in makeshift refugee camps, countless people paused their work, listening silently, tears glistening in their eyes—perhaps from sorrow, perhaps from excitement, perhaps… both.

title: The Broadcast Van on the Dirt Road
desc:
On a dusty dirt road, a GAZ truck painted with a striking red slogan (“State Care Delivered Home”) crawled slowly like a clumsy beetle. A large loudspeaker was mounted on its roof, and inside the cabin sat several young people in uniform, looking somewhat tired. They were members of the newly formed 'Urban-Rural Liaison Propaganda Work Team.' Their mission was to bring the 'voice from the Center' and some scarce supplies (mainly salt, soap, matches, and propaganda leaflets) to remote villages far from main roads, almost forgotten.

Today, they were headed to a small village called 'Muddy Hollow'—the name itself indicated the road conditions. The truck got stuck several times, forcing the team members to get out and push, getting covered in mud. The young team leader, Ilya, a passionate recent graduate from a pedagogical institute, felt a bit apprehensive looking out at the seemingly endless, somewhat desolate fields and scattered thatched huts. The 'close urban-rural integration, workers and peasants advancing hand-in-hand' described in textbooks seemed quite distant from the reality before him.

Finally, the truck swayed into Muddy Hollow. The village was quiet, except for a few skinny dogs barking warily. Some villagers in tattered clothes peeked out from their houses, observing these 'city folk' with a mixture of curiosity, numbness, and slight mistrust.

Ilya cleared his throat, turned on the loudspeaker on the roof, and began playing a pre-recorded broadcast: “Fellow villagers of Muddy Hollow! The Party and the state have not forgotten you! We bring you care and warmth…” The broadcast was enthusiastic, promising a wonderful future life: new roads, new schools, tractors, fertilizer…

The villagers gradually gathered, but mostly stood at a distance, listening silently. A white-haired old woman walked forward tremblingly, clutching an egg in her hand. “Kind people, can I trade this for some salt? Haven’t had salt at home for almost a month.”

Ilya quickly had a team member bring out salt, firmly refusing the old woman’s egg. “Grandma, this is distributed free by the state!” He tried hard to make his smile look sincere. The distribution of supplies was somewhat chaotic but quickly became orderly. The children were happiest; they received a small bar of soap, finding it incredibly novel.

Supplies distributed, broadcast finished. The truck started up again, heading to the next, even more remote village. Ilya looked back at Muddy Hollow and the villagers standing at the entrance watching them leave, his feelings mixed. The supplies they delivered might only alleviate hardship for a few days, and the promises in the broadcast sounded rather distant. But at least, they had come, brought information, made contact, breaking the long-standing isolation. Perhaps that was the meaning of it all.

title: Prosthetics and the Rehabilitation Center
desc:
On the outskirts of Minsk, a rehabilitation center converted from old military barracks filled the air with the smell of disinfectant and the faint sounds of various apparatus. It housed veterans and ordinary civilians who had lost limbs or suffered other severe disabilities during the war.

Seryozha, a young man in his early twenties, was gritting his teeth, trying to walk with his new, somewhat clumsy prosthetic leg. Sweat trickled down his forehead; each step felt like walking on knives. His left leg had been blown off by a German grenade during street fighting in Kyiv. When he woke up, he was already in a rear hospital, the leg that once let him run and play football gone forever.

Anna, a technician at the rehab center (whose husband had also died at the front), patiently supported him, encouraging him. “Try again, Seryozha! Step steady, yes, like that! You’re doing great!” Anna’s voice was gentle yet firm.

In the next room, several older veterans were learning to write or do simple crafts with prosthetic hands. One man, formerly a sniper, now struggled to thread a needle with a hook-like prosthesis. An atmosphere mixing pain, frustration, and stubborn hope permeated the air.

At night, Seryozha lay on his dormitory bed, staring blankly at the ceiling. Outside the window came the sounds of other rehabilitants moving about and occasional suppressed sobs. He missed his leg, missed the feeling of running, missed playing football with his buddies. He also feared the future. What could a one-legged man do? Could he still find work? Could he still marry and have children?

Anna came in, bringing him a cup of warm milk. “Can’t sleep?” she asked softly.

Seryozha nodded.

“Don’t lose heart, Seryozha,” Anna sat beside his bed. “You’re still young; losing a leg isn’t the end of the world. The country needs you, maybe not on the battlefield, but in the factories, in the fields, you are needed. They’ll teach you new skills here, fit you with the best prosthetics. You will stand up again, live again.” Her eyes shone with sincerity and a strength born only from enduring hardship.

Seryozha looked at Anna, then at the cold prosthetic leg beside his bed. Maybe she was right. The pain was real, the loss eternal, but life had to go on. Tomorrow, he would continue practicing walking, step by step, relearning how to stand on this land.

title: Shanties by the River
desc:
The icy wind off the Volga River blew through the makeshift shantytown on its banks, bringing biting cold. Varvara tightened the threadbare man's coat around her, trying to wrap her little son Ivan, huddled in her arms, more closely. They came from the distant Ural region, where terrible conflict and famine had occurred. They fled westward, hoping to find a livelihood in this land said to have 'restored order.'

People from all directions gathered here: Russian refugees like themselves, Central Asian nomads caught up in the war, Jewish survivors lucky enough to escape German concentration camps, and some unidentified drifters with wary eyes. They spoke different languages, had different pasts, their only commonality being poverty, hunger, and uncertainty about the future.

A fierce argument erupted from a nearby shack, apparently over a bit of firewood for heating. Varvara lowered her head, daring not to look. Order here was fragile; conflicts often broke out. The official relief station was overcrowded, and the distributed food was far from enough. She didn't know how much longer they could hold on here. Her husband had died of illness on the escape route; now only she and Ivan were left, relying on each other.

The sound of footsteps approached. A government worker in uniform, looking equally exhausted, came over, holding a registration book. “Name? Where from? Any special skills?” he asked robotically, without even looking up at Varvara.

Varvara gave her name and origin. As for skills… she shook her head; she only knew farming and housekeeping. The worker made a few marks in his book, then pointed towards a huge complex spewing black smoke in the distance. “Report there tomorrow. The city textile factory needs workers. They provide food, maybe housing too.” Without waiting for Varvara’s thanks, he hurried off to the next shack.

Varvara stared at the massive factory complex, her heart filled with both fear and a glimmer of hope. Go to a factory? She had never been inside one, didn't know what it was like. But at least, there would be food, a place to stay, maybe… maybe Ivan could survive.

title: The Roar of the Textile Mill
desc:
The textile mill workshop was deafening; thousands of old looms operated simultaneously, creating a roar like a waterfall. The air was thick with cotton lint, machine oil, and sweat. Varvara, along with dozens of other newly arrived female workers, was learning to operate these complex and dangerous-looking machines under the guidance of an expressionless female foreman.

Broken threads had to be quickly retied, jammed shuttles immediately dealt with. The slightest carelessness could result in fingers being injured by the moving machinery. This was incredibly difficult for Varvara; she was used to the openness of the fields and the solidity of the earth, while everything here made her feel dizzy and oppressed. Sweat streamed down her cheeks, mixing with cotton lint, itchy and uncomfortable.

The Tatar girl next to her, also new, seemed even less adapted, having already broken several shuttles and been harshly scolded by the foreman, her eyes red. Varvara wanted to comfort her, but the immense noise drowned out even her own voice.

Twelve hours of work each day, with only a half-hour break for meals. Food consisted of black bread, vegetable soup, and occasionally a tiny bit of salted fish. The dormitory was a large open room where dozens squeezed together, the air foul, snores constant. Wages were very low, barely enough for her and Ivan to survive.

But this was the best place she could find. At least, there was a roof over their heads, regular food rations, and Ivan had been placed in the factory nursery. Although conditions there were also basic, at least he was safe. Remembering the hungry, precarious days in the riverside shanty, she gritted her teeth and continued to focus on the rapidly operating machine before her. She had to learn, had to endure.

title: Relocation Notice
desc:
Varvara had just finished her shift and dragged her exhausted body back to the crowded dormitory when she saw a new notice posted on the wall. She couldn't read, so she grabbed a Russian girl from the same dorm who could. “Zoya, what does this say?”

Zoya read it to her: “Notice: To support key national construction projects and optimize labor resource allocation, upon decision by higher authorities, a portion of the staff and dependents from this factory will be transferred to work at the newly built Kuzbass Integrated Iron and Steel Works in… Siberia. The list of transferred personnel is as follows…”

The list was long. Zoya read for quite a while before finally reaching Varvara’s name.

“Go… to Siberia?” Varvara’s heart sank. She had just found a semblance of stability here, and now she was to be uprooted again, sent to that legendary land of ice, snow, and desolation? “Why me?”

“The notice says priority is given to… uh… personnel with ‘simple social connections, no local ties.’” Zoya looked at her with some sympathy. “Also, comrades with experience in rural life and ability to endure hardship will be prioritized…”

Varvara understood. A widow like her, with a child, no relatives, was precisely the easiest target for ‘optimized allocation.’ She felt as if she were back on the road fleeing, helpless, pushed forward by an immense force towards a completely unknown direction.

“Can I refuse to go?” she asked, trembling.

Zoya shook her head. “The notice says this is the nation’s need, a glorious task. Refusal… will have serious consequences.”

That night, Varvara held Ivan close, unable to sleep. She didn’t know what Siberia was like, how dangerous the steel mill work would be, whether they could adapt to the climate. She only knew they were on the move again. She hugged her son tightly, as if he were the only real thing she could hold onto.

title: Ghost in the Cellar
desc:
“Is it clear inside?” Captain Petrov wiped sweat from his brow, asking the two soldiers who had just emerged from the cellar of the abandoned farmhouse. This was a small village not far from Moscow; intelligence suggested a fugitive former low-ranking officer of the SS 'Wiking' Division might be hiding here.

“Report, sir! Empty! Just some moldy potatoes and a few dead rats,” one soldier replied, dusting himself off.

Petrov frowned. This was the third location they had searched based on that unreliable tip-off. The war had been over for so long, yet these Nazi remnants were like ghosts, either long gone or hidden deeper than rabbits. Capturing them was pure luck.

“Let’s move out,” he waved his hand, about to give the order to leave, when suddenly a faint noise came from the depths of the cellar. Everyone instantly tensed, raising their weapons.

“Who’s there?! Come out! Or we’ll shoot!” Petrov cried sharply.

After a long moment, an extremely emaciated, ragged old man, almost unrecognizable as human, emerged from the darkness, hands raised above his head, trembling violently. His eyes were vacant, muttering incomprehensible words, seemingly German, yet perhaps not.

The soldiers immediately subdued him. A search revealed only a blurry photograph, apparently of family, tucked in his inner pocket, with a few illegible letters written on the back.

“Who is he? Is he the one we’re looking for?” Petrov asked the accompanying local guide, a taciturn old hunter.

The old hunter examined him closely, then shook his head. “Doesn’t look like it. Seems like a madman who’s been hiding in the woods for a long time, maybe some straggler German soldier, or… someone else.”

Petrov looked at this ghost-like captive, feeling a wave of annoyance. “Take him, hand him over to the higher-ups for processing,” he said. Whether a genuine Nazi remnant or a pitiful relic of the war, it no longer mattered. What mattered was completing the mission, erasing these ‘unstable elements’ from the map.

title: Echoes Beneath the Geologist's Hammer
desc:
“So, Dmitri Ivanovich, can you really knock tanks out from under this rock?” Private Sasha asked, rubbing his freezing hands, looking at the bearded geologist before him, who looked like he’d just emerged from a bear’s den. They stood on a remote slope in the Ural Mountains, the biting wind making their faces sting.

Dmitri Ivanovich didn’t answer directly. He caressed the mineral sample glistening with metallic luster with his rough fingers, his eyes blazing with the fervor of a believer who had found the Holy Grail. “Tanks? Sasha, my boy, this is much more potent than tanks! This is nickel, this is tungsten, good stuff for making cannon barrels and armor-piercing shells! With this, our ‘Iron Fist’ can smash the turtle shells of those Western capitalists and Eastern samurai!” He pulled out his ancestral silver flask, took a large swig of homemade spirit, and choked, tears streaming.

“The war is over, Professor,” Sasha cautiously reminded him. “We need tractors and reinforcing bars for building houses now.”

“War never truly ends, Sasha! Not as long as imperialism and exploitation exist!” The geologist waved his hammer, spittle flying. “We will turn every stone here into a bullet aimed at the enemy! We will make these sleeping mountains contribute their final treasures to our great motherland!” He looked around; only the howling wind and a few other soldiers, equally freezing and bewildered, were present.

“But… we barely have enough trucks to haul these stones down the mountain,” Sasha muttered.

“We will have them! Everything will be provided!” The geologist waved his hand grandly, as if a steel torrent could immediately flow into the valley at his command. “The report will state: Discovery of strategic-grade rare metal deposits! Enormous potential! Recommend extraction at all costs! For the strength of the motherland!” He shouldered his hammer like a victorious general. “Let’s go! Back for hot soup! Tomorrow, we dig again! For our great… well… just dig!”

title: German Letters in the Mine Pit
desc:
The mining area south of Tula was once an important coal supplier for the 'Reichskommissariat Moskowien.' Now, the creak of the mine hoist sounded again, only the faces operating the machinery and digging coal underground were Russian. Boris, a former tractor driver, now the mine's production dispatcher, frowned over an old mine map marked bilingually in German and Russian.

“These damn Germans dug really deep,” an old miner, his face covered in coal dust, peered over. “Some tunnels, even they didn't know where they led, like rat holes.”

“Orders from above are to restore production in all usable seams,” Boris sighed. “Doesn’t matter who dug it; it’s our country’s wealth now. But look at this map, many places are marked ‘Dangerous’ or ‘Flooded,’ and some even have skulls drawn… Who dares go down?”

A young engineer nearby whispered, “I heard from the technical department that when the Germans retreated, they might have tampered with some abandoned tunnels… set traps or… something else.”

Boris’s heart tightened. This mine wasn't just about coal; it could also harbor danger. “Strengthen safety inspections!” he ordered immediately. “Anyone going down must go in pairs, carry gas detectors! Report any suspicious findings immediately! We’re here to mine coal for national construction, not to be buried alive for the German devils!”

The miners’ expressions turned serious too. They knew this land beneath their feet, even after liberation, still held the shadows and dangers of war. Every descent was not just a struggle with rock and coal seams, but also a gamble against a dark history. Mining lamps flickered in the dark tunnels, illuminating faint German letter markings on the mottled rock walls, seeming to silently narrate past evils and present risks.

title: Poplars by the Riverbank
desc:
On the middle reaches of the Volga River, construction of a massive dam was in full swing. Bulldozers, excavators, and heavy trucks moved ceaselessly, transforming the riverbank into a giant construction site. According to the plan, a huge artificial lake would form here, and downstream, a powerful hydroelectric power station would be built, providing electricity and irrigation water for the surrounding industry and agriculture.

Old fisherman Ivan Kuzmich sat in his small boat, casting his net for the last time. His little wooden hut, along with the entire fishing village inhabited for generations, would soon be submerged by the rising river waters. The government gave them some compensation money, promised to allocate new houses in a newly built resettlement site, and said they could raise fish in the reservoir later.

But he still couldn't let go. Couldn't let go of this river that had nurtured him and his ancestors, couldn't let go of the old poplar trees by the bank that had watched him grow up, couldn't let go of the misty water vapor at dusk and the calls of returning water birds. All this would soon sink beneath the water, becoming a new blue area on a map and a power generation figure.

Deafening explosions echoed from the distance; the engineering team was clearing the riverbed. Ivan sighed and began hauling in his net. It held only a few small fish, some weeds, and silt. He looked at the murky river water and the rapidly rising concrete dam on the opposite bank, feeling empty inside.

He knew the country needed electricity, needed water conservancy, needed development. Personal feelings and nostalgia seemed insignificant before the grand slogan of 'transforming nature to benefit the people.' But he just couldn't understand why it had to be this way. Couldn't they leave a little more space for the river and the people living by it? Oars cut through the water, carrying the old man and his last catch, slowly rowing towards his disappearing home. The old poplar trees swayed in the wind, as if bidding a final farewell.

title: New Landmarks Under the Cranes
desc:
Central Moscow, areas once ravaged by war, were now transforming at an astonishing pace. Giant cranes, like steel giraffes, hoisted prefabricated concrete components onto the skeletons of modern high-rises rapidly ascending. Wide avenues were being paved, and new metro lines were under intense construction.

Anna Ivanovna, an elderly saleswoman who had worked in a nearby department store for decades, passed through this vast construction site every day on her way to and from work. She remembered what it looked like before the war—the elegant old buildings, the small alleys full of life. The war turned them into heaps of rubble. Now, the rubble was cleared, replaced by these square, clean-lined, seemingly identical new buildings.

“How grand!” exclaimed Lena, her young colleague walking with her, her eyes sparkling with anticipation for the future. “I heard there will be cinemas, ice rinks, and even shops selling foreign goods here later! When it's finished, we must come and see!”

Anna just smiled without speaking. She admitted the new buildings looked more 'modern,' and were more spacious and bright. Saying goodbye to those dark, damp old houses was a good thing. Yet, she always felt these new buildings lacked something—lacked the charm that came with time and human touch. Walking on these wide, straight, but similar streets, she sometimes felt a sense of unfamiliarity and disorientation.

She missed the old Moscow, a bit crowded, a bit chaotic, but full of the vibrancy of life. The Moscow where you could buy freshly baked hot bread from a corner shop, where you could chat with neighbors while hanging laundry in the courtyard. Now, everything was becoming bigger, faster, more… standardized. Was this progress? Perhaps. But in her heart, a small part always yearned for those marks of the past Moscow, forever erased by cranes and bulldozers.

title: Guitar Sounds on the Arbat
desc:
Arbat Street was slowly awakening. Some storefronts were repainted, sporting new signs—a state-run bookstore, a cooperative café, even a small gallery labeled 'Art Salon,' though the works displayed inside were mostly landscapes and 'mainstream' portraits.

In the evening, a young man with long hair and old jeans sat on a bench by the street, strumming a chipped old guitar and singing softly to himself. He sang a folk ballad tinged with melancholy and confusion, the lyrics subtly hinting at loss, searching, and uncertainty about the future. His voice wasn't loud, nor his technique particularly refined, but the slightly husky voice and sincere emotion drew a few passersby to stop and listen.

Among them were workers just off shift, students in uniform, and a man with glasses carrying a briefcase who looked like an intellectual. No one spoke; they just listened quietly. The guitar sounds and singing drifted on the early summer evening breeze, mingling with the distant car horns and pedestrians' chatter, creating a somewhat strange yet intensely real Arbat twilight scene.

A plainclothes man in a grey trench coat with sharp eyes (perhaps responsible for maintaining order, perhaps something else) stood nearby for a while, ultimately did nothing, and turned away.

The young man finished his last song, strummed a final, lingering chord. No one applauded, but the intellectual-looking man stepped forward and dropped a few small-denomination rubles into his open guitar case. “Well sung,” he said quietly. “Haven't heard a song like that in a long time.” The young man looked up, giving him a shy, grateful smile. Night deepened, the neon lights of Arbat Street began to flicker, illuminating this ancient street searching for its new voice.

title: Whispers by the Neva
desc:
“Petrograd… no, Leningrad… what should it be called now?” Yevgeny Andreyevich, a white-haired old professor, stood in the restored Palace Square, gazing at the Admiralty spire opposite, blackened by war but still standing tall, muttering to himself. The city’s name, like its fate, had changed several times amidst the storms of history. Now, official circles seemed inclined to restore the old name 'Saint Petersburg,' but for the older generation like him, who had endured the Siege and starvation, the name 'Leningrad' was already fused with the city's soul, unforgettable.

His student, a lively girl named Katya, took his arm. “Professor, don’t dwell on it so much. A name is just a symbol. What matters is that the city is being reborn, isn’t it? Look, the shops on Nevsky Prospekt are open, the theaters are staging performances again!”

Yevgeny nodded. Yes, the city was repairing the scars of war at an astonishing speed. Bombed bridges were reconnected, church spires sheared off by shells were being scaffolded, and tour boats reappeared on the Neva. Yet he always felt that beneath this surface of recovery lay an unspoken weariness and neglected grievances.

Compared to the resources poured into the capital, Moscow, this hero city seemed to receive too little attention. Many important cultural heritage sites were being restored slowly, research institutions remained underfunded, and the aftereffects of the Siege—both physical and psychological—were far from adequately addressed. “Moscow celebrates victory, plans a magnificent future,” he sighed inwardly, “but do they still remember how much blood we shed here, how much hunger and cold we endured?”

Katya seemed to sense his thoughts. “Professor, a few days ago the university organized us to lay flowers at Piskaryovskoye Memorial Cemetery,” she said softly. “We won’t forget. This city is always our pride.”

Yevgeny looked at the girl's clear, determined eyes, feeling a flicker of warmth. Perhaps hope lay with these young people. They hadn’t lived through the darkest years, but they carried the city's memory and spirit. As long as memory survived, as long as the Neva flowed silently, the cry of Saint Petersburg (or Leningrad) would eventually be heard.

His student, a lively girl named Katya, took his arm. “Professor, don’t dwell on it so much. A name is just a symbol. What matters is that the city is being reborn, isn’t it? Look, the shops on Nevsky Prospekt are open, the theaters are staging performances again!”

Yevgeny nodded. Yes, the city was repairing the scars of war at an astonishing speed. Bombed bridges were reconnected, church spires sheared off by shells were being scaffolded, and tour boats reappeared on the Neva. Yet he always felt that beneath this surface of recovery lay an unspoken weariness and neglected grievances.

Compared to the resources poured into the capital, Moscow, this hero city seemed to receive too little attention. Many important cultural heritage sites were being restored slowly, research institutions remained underfunded, and the aftereffects of the Siege—both physical and psychological—were far from adequately addressed. “Moscow celebrates victory, plans a magnificent future,” he sighed inwardly, “but do they still remember how much blood we shed here, how much hunger and cold we endured?”

Katya seemed to sense his thoughts. “Professor, a few days ago the university organized us to lay flowers at Piskaryovskoye Memorial Cemetery,” she said softly. “We won’t forget. This city is always our pride.”

Yevgeny looked at the girl's clear, determined eyes, feeling a flicker of warmth. Perhaps hope lay with these young people. They hadn’t lived through the darkest years, but they carried the city's memory and spirit. As long as memory survived, as long as the Neva flowed silently, the cry of Saint Petersburg (or Leningrad) would eventually be heard.

title: Whispers in the Laboratory
desc:
Zelenograd, the area outside Moscow designated as the future 'Science City.' In a newly built laboratory, its windows still covered with protective film, several young engineers huddled around a computer prototype imported (or rather, dismantled and copied) from a 'friendly country,' arguing in low voices.

“This logic gate design is clearly flawed! Signal interference is too severe!” exclaimed a young man with thick glasses and messy hair, waving a sheet covered in complex circuit diagrams.

“But Volodya, we don't have a better alternative! Imported components are too expensive, and impossible to get! We can only make do with existing domestic components and try to improve them!” countered a slightly older, seemingly calmer engineer.

“Make do? Can ‘making do’ create world-class chips? Can it catch up with the Americans and Japanese? The order from above is strict: we must produce results quickly, achieve the ‘Silicon Dream’!” Volodya's face flushed red.

The laboratory head, a taciturn middle-aged expert said to have worked at a top-secret nuclear physics institute, walked over and patted Volodya’s shoulder. “Calm down, comrades. You eat an elephant one bite at a time; you walk a path one step at a time. Our foundation is weak, we started late, that’s a fact. But we have brains, we have drive, and… the full support of the state.” He pointed to the slogan on the wall: “Self-Reliance, Strive for Strength, Overtake World Advanced Levels!”

“But what good are slogans? The equipment isn't good enough, the materials aren't good enough, even a stable power supply isn't guaranteed!” Volodya remained unconvinced.

“That’s precisely why we need to create the conditions, overcome the difficulties!” the head stated firmly. “When we developed the atomic bomb back then, conditions were much worse, didn't we succeed? What the Japanese can do, why can’t we Russians do it? We might not be able to completely copy their path, but we can forge our own!” His words held an undeniable confidence and resilience.

The engineers gradually calmed down, gathered around the prototype again, and began discussing improvement plans. Outside, new laboratory buildings were under construction. The setting sun cast a golden hue over this land brimming with hope and challenges.

title: Gazing from Mamayev Kurgan
desc:
On the banks of the Volga, Mamayev Kurgan. The colossal statue 'The Motherland Calls,' having undergone restoration, once again raised its sword high, standing on the city's commanding height, overlooking the hero city reborn from rubble below—Volgograd.

Retired old worker Ivan Petrovich climbed this hill every week, visiting this quiet memorial cemetery where countless martyrs lay buried. He would place a bouquet of wildflowers (secretly picked from the park) before an unmarked soldier's grave, then sit on the stone steps nearby, silently smoking a cigarette, gazing at the city below and the winding Volga.

He knew almost everyone buried here—not by name, but by their stories. They were his comrades-in-arms, his neighbors, his relatives. They fought and died on this land, exchanging their lives for the city's present day. The city below had changed greatly; new factories were built, new residential areas appeared, streets widened. Newspapers reported that Volgograd was becoming an important national industrial and transportation hub, with a bright future.

But Ivan always felt that the city's voice seemed somewhat forgotten. People talked more about production targets, construction plans, new policies from Moscow, the wonderful future life. Discussions about steadfastness, sacrifice, and the indomitable spirit this city represented seemed to be diminishing. Children knew about the Battle of Stalingrad, but did they know what it felt like to starve, freeze, and face death here back then? Did they know that under every stone in this city might lie the bones of heroes?

He sometimes whispered to those unmarked graves, as if chatting with old friends. Telling them about the changes below, sharing his worries. The wind sighed across the hill, like the responding voices of the departed souls. Volgograd could not just be an industrial city; it should forever be a beacon of the Russian national spirit. Its voice—that voice of sacrifice, resilience, and unyielding spirit—should be forever remembered, forever proclaimed.

title: Debate Over Textbooks
desc:
Moscow Ministry of Education, meeting room of the History Textbook Compilation Committee. The atmosphere was somewhat tense. Tables were piled high with historical documents, archival excerpts, and draft textbooks. The committee members—venerable historians, political officers from the military, and officials from the Ministry responsible for ideology—were engaged in a fierce debate over the narrative approach for the section on the 'Great Patriotic War and National Unification' in the new primary and secondary school history textbooks.

“I believe we must truthfully reflect the brutality of the war, including our initial heavy losses and certain command errors,” said an old professor wearing reading glasses, his tone earnest. “Only by facing history squarely can we draw genuine lessons.”

“Truthfully reflect?” A military officer with stars on his shoulder boards frowned. “Does that mean also writing about the routs and defections of certain units? About the chaos in the rear and certain erroneous decisions? This will shake the younger generation’s confidence in our cause! I believe we should focus more on heroism, the people’s resistance, and the final great victory!”

“But excessive beautification of history is equally dangerous!” countered another scholar from a university. “That will make us forget past sufferings and repeat mistakes! We cannot only talk about victory without talking about the cost!”

“The cost must be mentioned, but the main theme must be bright, positive, and uplifting!” The Ministry official responsible for ideology tapped the table, trying to control the situation. “History serves the present! Our primary task now is to unite the people, consolidate unity, stimulate patriotic enthusiasm and the drive to build the nation! The textbook must reflect this!”

The debate reached an impasse. How to narrate that complex period, filled with both pain and glory? What should be remembered, what should be downplayed, and what should be reinterpreted? This was not just an academic question, but a political issue concerning national identity and the future direction. Sunlight streamed through the windows, but the air in the meeting room felt heavy. The final draft would profoundly affect an entire generation’s understanding of the past, and their imagination of the future.

title: Symphony of the Assembly Line
desc:
In a newly built, massive consolidated factory in the Ural region, several different production lines were operating at an unprecedented scale and efficiency. From raw material input to finished product output, various stages were precisely calculated and connected, forming a grand and complex industrial panorama. Equipment and workers originally scattered among several smaller surrounding factories were concentrated here under unified management and production.

Igor, formerly a key technician in one of those small factories, was now the section chief of this brand-new bearing production line. Standing in the elevated control room, he overlooked the busy yet orderly assembly line below. The roar of machinery, the rotation of conveyor belts, the friction of metal—all merged into a unique symphony of the industrial age.

The benefits of centralization were obvious: unified procurement of raw materials reduced costs; standardized production processes improved efficiency and product quality; centralized worker management facilitated training and deployment. The numbers on the reports were dazzling; output climbed steadily, and the defect rate continued to fall. Higher leadership was very satisfied and had already designated this place as a 'model of industrial modernization reform.'

But Igor also harbored some hidden worries. Back in the small factory, everyone knew each other, like a big family; problems could be discussed and solved at any time. Now, with hundreds or thousands of workers, mostly strangers, and multiple management levels, the stench of bureaucracy was growing stronger. A small technical innovation idea required reporting through layers of hierarchy; by the time approval came, it was too late. Workers felt more like replaceable parts on an assembly line than living human beings. The 'workshop spirit,' full of human warmth, that existed in the old small factories was disappearing.

He saw a young worker being harshly reprimanded by the team leader for an operational error; people nearby lowered their heads, pretending not to see. Igor frowned and picked up his walkie-talkie: “Team Leader Three, pay attention to your work methods; be patient when guiding new comrades.” Efficiency had improved, but the distance between people seemed to have widened. Was this really the 'modernization' they wanted? He didn't know. He only knew that this symphony of the assembly line would continue to roar.

title: Nylon Stockings at the Market
desc:
Izmaylovo Market, once merely a place to exchange black bread and potato peels, now seemed magically revitalized. Sunlight streamed through the repaired glass roof, illuminating dazzling stalls: piles of sausages (though mostly made of potato flour and unidentified meat, they at least looked like sausages), vividly colored, almost unreal printed fabrics, and… heavens, brand new nylon stockings!

Old tailor Yevgeny Pavlovich, his hands trembling, picked up a pair of gossamer-thin silk stockings, examining them carefully against the sunlight. He could hardly believe his eyes. Just a few years ago, forget nylon stockings, even finding a decent piece of cotton thread was difficult. Back then, people wore patched old uniforms, made ropes from birch bark, and burned furniture for heating in winter. And now… shop windows displayed radios and new-style kettles, brightly painted small cars (though still few, and mostly state-owned) drove on the streets, even the black bread from the neighboring bakery seemed less gritty than before.

“What’s wrong, old man?” Sasha, the young lad selling second-hand army boots nearby, sauntered over, a cigarette dangling from his lips. “Fancied this women’s stuff? Planning to buy it back for your old lady as a surprise?”

Yevgeny put down the stockings, shaking his head, then nodding. “Yes, Sasha, a surprise… and a shock.” He touched his own coat, still bearing several patches. “It all came so quickly, so fast it makes one anxious. Yesterday we were digging for food in the rubble, today we can buy nylon stockings? This money… is it real? These goods… where did they suddenly appear from?”

Sasha shrugged. “Who cares! As long as there’s money to be made, goods to sell, and life goes on, right? The higher-ups said this is an ‘economic miracle’! It’s because we Russians are hardworking, and the state policy is good! You should be happy, old man!”

Yevgeny looked at Sasha’s young, carefree face, then at the bustling crowd in the market, their faces mixture of hope and bewilderment. Maybe Sasha was right; life was indeed getting better, so fast it felt like an unreal dream. Factories were hiring, wages were rising, once-empty shelves were slowly being filled. What lay behind this ‘miracle’? A smarter plan, harder labor, or… some other force he didn't know? He stopped thinking about it. He took out the crumpled rubles he had saved for months, carefully counted out a few bills, and bought the nylon stockings. Perhaps his old wife would be genuinely happy wearing them. In this world that felt almost too good to be true, a little bit of small, real happiness was always good.

title: Gazing at the Stars
desc:
The main building of the restored Moscow State University regained its imposing yet somewhat oppressive silhouette in the evening glow. The red star atop the spire had been polished anew, gleaming faintly in the twilight.

Andrei, a third-year architecture student, sat with his classmate Olga on the steps of the square before the main building, rapidly sketching the lines of this behemoth in his sketchbook.

“It’s incredible, isn’t it?” Olga paused her pencil, sighing. “It’s so tall, so vast, like a mountain. Building it back then must have cost countless manpower and resources.” Her tone held both admiration and an subtle complex emotion.

“Yes,” Andrei also put down his pencil, leaning back against the cool stone steps. “My grandfather participated in its construction. He said conditions were extremely harsh then; many people collapsed from exhaustion on the site.” He paused. “Later… the Germans came. They supposedly used it as one of their important command posts too. You can still find bullet holes and traces of graffiti on the walls now, though they’ve been carefully repaired.”

These 'sister' buildings, along with several other towers scattered across Moscow, stood like silent giants, witnessing the city’s, and indeed the country’s, most turbulent, glorious, and painful years. They were symbols of an era’s ambition, embodiments of powerful will, and also the crystallization of countless ordinary people’s sweat and even blood. Now, the war was over, flags had changed, yet they still stood there, like huge, indelible question marks left by history.

“The teacher said there are plans now to convert some of them into luxury hotels or office buildings, to attract foreign investment,” Olga said softly. “Do you think… it’s appropriate?”

Andrei didn’t answer immediately. He gazed up at the spire piercing the clouds, the star atop it shining exceptionally bright in the deepening night sky. “Who knows,” he finally said. “Maybe they no longer need to represent a certain ideology or a certain leader. Maybe they can just be… buildings. Part of the city skyline, reminding us where we came from, and also where we need to go.” He picked up his pencil again. “At least, they’re still there, for us to look up at.”

title: I Have Returned, Mother
desc:
Vadim, thirty-six years old, former infantry sergeant, now… someone who could finally be called a 'Moscow resident.' He stood on Red Square, surrounded by the bustling crowd, the smooth cobblestones beneath his feet. Pigeons fluttered around him; the melodious bells of St. Basil's Cathedral chimed from its onion domes in the distance. Warm sunlight bathed his face, dispelling the last lingering chill from the Siberian POW camp.

Twenty years. Twenty whole years. He had left Moscow a young lad, full of patriotic fervor, following his unit westward, and then… came the rout, encirclement, capture. In icy Siberia, amidst endless hard labor and hunger, he almost believed he would never return. Moscow became a distant, hazy, yet incredibly warm dream in his memory. There was the courtyard where he played as a child, the taste of his mother’s borscht, the riverbank where he first secretly held a girl's hand.

Now, he was back. But the Moscow before him was both familiar and strange. Red Square was still there, the Kremlin walls still imposing, but the colors of St. Basil’s seemed faded, bearing scars from shrapnel. The GUM department store windows were no longer empty, displaying some colorful goods he had never seen before. People on the streets dressed more neatly, their expressions less perpetually tense, but deep in their eyes seemed hidden scars they preferred not to touch.

He walked aimlessly along familiar streets, trying to find his childhood home. The narrow alley was still there, but the original wooden house was gone, replaced by a brand new, seemingly characterless Khrushchev-era building. He stood before that building for a long time, until a curious child ran up and asked whom he was looking for.

He didn't answer, just slowly turned and walked towards the Moscow River. The river still flowed quietly, reflecting the outlines of buildings under repair and newly constructed ones on both banks. The river breeze touched his face, carrying the city's unique scent—a mixture of dust, car exhaust, and the气息 of some new life.

He reached the riverbank, took off the old army boots that had carried him across half of Russia, and stepped barefoot onto the cool earth. The soil was soft yet firm. He slowly bent down, reached out his hands, covered in calluses and scars, and gently touched the ground beneath his feet.

This was it. No matter what it had become, no matter how much suffering it had endured, this was home. This was Moscow, the heart of Russia, the place he had dreamed of for twenty years.

He looked up, at this familiar yet strange river before him, at this city awakening, striving to escape its nightmare. He knew too much had been lost, never to be recovered. His youth, his comrades, the home in his memory… But at least, he was back. He was alive. This land still existed.

He took a deep breath, as if wanting to inhale the very essence of this land into his lungs. Then, he opened his arms, as if to embrace the river, the city, this land, so weathered yet so resilient. Like a long-lost child finally falling into his mother’s embrace, tears streamed silently, soaking the earth beneath his feet, the earth that held all his memories and hopes. He hugged this earth, as if having made a firm resolution. He would live here, watch this city truly recover, make up for those lost years.

He stood before that building for a long time, until a curious child ran up and asked whom he was looking for.

He didn't answer, just slowly turned and walked towards the Moscow River. The river still flowed quietly, reflecting the outlines of buildings under repair and newly constructed ones on both banks. The river breeze touched his face, carrying the city's unique scent—a mixture of dust, car exhaust, and the气息 of some new life.

He reached the riverbank, took off the old army boots that had carried him across half of Russia, and stepped barefoot onto the cool earth. The soil was soft yet firm. He slowly bent down, reached out his hands, covered in calluses and scars, and gently touched the ground beneath his feet.

This was it. No matter what it had become, no matter how much suffering it had endured, this was home. This was Moscow, the heart of Russia, the place he had dreamed of for twenty years.

He looked up, at this familiar yet strange river before him, at this city awakening, striving to escape its nightmare. He knew too much had been lost, never to be recovered. His youth, his comrades, the home in his memory… But at least, he was back. He was alive. This land still existed.

He took a deep breath, as if wanting to inhale the very essence of this land into his lungs. Then, he opened his arms, as if to embrace the river, the city, this land, so weathered yet so resilient. Like a long-lost child finally falling into his mother’s embrace, tears streamed silently, soaking the earth beneath his feet, the earth that held all his memories and hopes. He hugged this earth, as if having made a firm resolution. He would live here, watch this city truly recover, make up for those lost years.
